Soren Colding wasn't expecting the call. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes.

Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team.

The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome.

It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top.

This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place.

"Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane.

Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room.

"There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch.

"Then I saw all the other guys on round tables - they were sitting with their agents, their wives, their family, their friends in normal [clothes]. Then the Danish guy turned in. Nobody knows who he is, in his Adidas training suit!"

Colding struck up a friendship with South Africa defender David Nyathi and the pair where whisked off to a 45-minute training session that afternoon. Not all the big names took part, but one Argentine offered a taste of what was to come.

"Batistuta was there and just to see him and his moves, you thought, 'Okay, it's gonna be a nice evening tomorrow'," remembers Colding, who also got to link up with European boss Franz Beckenbauer.

"He was pretty cool. He was saying, 'what is your position? Defender? OK, can you play left defender?' No problem - I'll play wherever you place me!"

Ronaldo scored twice and assisted three more goals as Rest of the World beat their Europe counterparts 5-2 in Marseille

Come game day, 38,000 fans packed in to see peak Ronaldo. Months earlier, Il Fenomeno completed a world-record move to Inter Milan on the back of 47 goals in 49 games in one sensational season at Barcelona.

The 23-year-old was the most exciting player on the planet.

"It was crazy, actually," recalls Colding, who previously faced the forward when Denmark's under-21s played Brazil in Florianopolis before the 1996 Olympics.

"That was almost the same team as they played with at the World Cup in '98. So we lost 5-1. Just to see his speed and how he played - I played against Roberto Carlos in that game as well - that was just another level. I thought, 'what is going on here?'

"When I saw him there again, it was just to see what is actually reachable for a football player, because that was next level tremendous. His speed and his touch are unbelievable, and also his power.

"And still, just a small, shy guy. You know, he just wants to play football, and all these people are around him protecting him. Just to see when a star like him joins an event like that, how many people around him, agents and followers, how should you navigate all that?"

Ronaldo, captaining Carlos Alberto Parreira's side, was at his blistering best, scoring twice and setting up the other three as Rest of the World won 5-2 - Batistuta also netted twice, before Zidane responded.

"You start thinking what if you injured some of them," explains Colding. "You are a defender, you don't want goals against you, so you have to fight - that's how I am.

"How hard should you go to them? Should you just let them go? No. I would not just let them run and score. I tried to do my best, that was probably not good enough!"

Diego Maradona featured for a Rest of the World XI in August 1987 - a year after Argentina beat England at the World Cup

This wasn't the first outing for a World XI, in fact such Fifa exhibition matches had been taking place since England hosted an all-star side in front of a reported 100,000 fans at Wembley in 1963 to celebrate the Football Association's centenary.

They became a semi-regular occurrence as testimonials or charity fixtures, with huge names appearing across eras from Eusebio and Zico to Roberto Baggio.

But the biggest coup was arguably luring Diego Maradona to Wembley a year after winning the World Cup with Argentina and scoring his 'Hand of God' goal against England.

Jon Smith, who represented the Napoli star, explains in his book 'The Deal' how Maradona was offered around £250,000 and flown from Naples on a private jet to take part in an anniversary game against the Football League.

"In fairness, he wanted to shake hands with the team and say 'sorry if I offended you'," Smith tells BBC Sport. "He genuinely believed his talent was God-given.

"He was sort of two people. He was lovely, Diego, when you were with him. When he crossed the white line he was Maradona. So the Hand of God was an expression of 'I am God's footballing representative', if you like.

"It was madness, because you can imagine how the media were all over it. It was a bit special."

Napoli and Argentina welcomed the opportunity for Maradona to generate some good PR in England, helped by Bobby Robson's Football League side winning 3-0 - Bryan Robson netting twice and Norman Whiteside grabbing the other.

"I remember introducing him to Bobby Robson," adds Smith. "He put his hand out, and Bobby said 'I'm not shaking that hand!', which I thought was lovely - he did shake the other hand!"

A Ronaldinho XI beat their Shevchenko counterparts 6-3 in February 2005 - Ronaldinho, Samuel Eto'o, Alessandro Del Piero and Gianfranco Zola were all on the scoresheet

One of the final games saw a Ronaldinho XI take on a Shevchenko XI at Nou Camp in February 2005 to raise funds for victims of the 2004 tsunami.

Andriy Shevchenko's stacked squad included Zidane, David Beckham, Alessandro Del Piero, Thierry Henry, Raul, Paolo Maldini and Steven Gerrard.

Ronaldinho could call on Ronaldo, Kaka, Cafu, Adriano, Javier Zanetti, Didier Drogba and Samuel Eto'o, though it was Southampton's Henri Camara who scored twice in a 6-3 win for the Brazilian's team.

But things have moved on, and it is hard to imagine clubs releasing their star players for such an exhibition nowadays.

"The whole world of football has changed," says Smith. "You used to have testimonial games and testimonial years because players got paid okay but by the same token weren't earning £100k a week.

"It wouldn't happen now because the business of football is so much bigger, you can't risk the players - if they get injured playing for their country, that annoys everybody.

"But beyond that they are owned by big corporations and in some cases countries, so you just wouldn't allow your player to go out and do that."

Colding went on to play 27 times for Denmark, featuring at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, but retains fond memories of representing the Europe XI.

"Now, to come up with the idea to make a game like this, in combination with the draw, I think everyone will say you are crazy," explains Colding.

"But at that time it was perfectly planned and a fantastic event to be a part of. As players, we have a tremendous relationship between each other.

"It shows all the spectators you can be enemies on the field, but you can actually be friends and gather together in this kind of event.

"That for me sends a signal to all that we are a community in football and we can actually make great things together that not only is a question of money."

In fact, he still has his Europe shirt - a reminder of coming up against Ronaldo and Batistuta and being a team-mate of Zidane almost 30 years ago.

"It doesn't smell very good, actually," laughs Colding. "Sometimes, when I go in the garage with my kids and tell them about it and what actually happened, I see in their eyes, they don't really believe that I was a part of that game.

"That was not about money - we didn't get anything to join - it was just because you represent your country, so it was a great experience, it's also about having fun.

"You know, as small kids, you don't start by saying, 'I want to earn 20 million'. No, you start because it's fun to play football."

Canadian authorities say organised vehicle theft is a serious crime threatening the security of communities

Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.

They are accused of stealing luxury vehicles and shipping them to West Africa.

Police in Peel, Ontario said they had recovered 96 high-value vehicles concealed in shipping containers. The vehicles, valued at $4.5m (£3.4m) were destined for export via Canadian ports.

The suspects face 231 charges, with arrest warrants issued for others. Police say some of the accused may face deportation after their criminal proceedings are concluded.

The arrests followed months of what police described as an "extensive auto theft investigation".

The investigations began in March in partnership with Canada's border agency after police identified a warehouse allegedly being used to store stolen vehicles.

Investigators believe the network was led by five people who coordinated the theft, transportation and export of the stolen vehicles, with the others playing supporting roles.

"Together, investigators linked the network to loading sites, container movements and the transportation of stolen re-VINed vehicles," the police said in a statement.

Re-VINing is the illegal practice of altering the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) to conceal its identity and make it harder to trace.

Canadian authorities have described organised vehicle theft as a growing threat, saying it was linked to wider criminal networks.

"Organised auto theft is a predatory business model run by transnational syndicates that terrorise families and fund broader criminal enterprises," Peel Regional Police Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich said.

The trafficking of vehicles from North America and Europe to African countries has been a long-standing concern for law enforcement agencies.

Last year, Interpol said more than 100 luxury vehicles stolen from Canada and European countries had been recovered, exposing a network involved in trafficking stolen cars to West Africa.

In a separate operation the same year, Ghanaian security authorities recovered 43 luxury vehicles stolen from Europe and North America.

They attributed the success of the operation to improved cooperation between national and international law enforcement agencies.

A single meteor streaks across the starry night sky during the annual Leonid meteor shower

The Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak on Tuesday night, giving UK sky gazers their best chance to see it this year.

The celestial spectacle runs until 30 November, but the greatest activity is expected on the night of Tuesday 17 November, into the early hours of Wednesday.

There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.

The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.

These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second, meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.

Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.

The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.

However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark, perhaps 20 or 30 minutes, will give you the best chance of spotting them.

A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.

Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant, the point from which they seem to appear, will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze. Leo does not rise until around midnight, so the best time to look is after midnight and in the hours before dawn.

As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.

Viewing conditions could be particularly good around the peak. The Moon will set at around 23:30 GMT on Tuesday, meaning its reflected light is less likely to spoil the view in the hours after midnight.

The best chance of seeing the Leonids will be in the far north of Scotland, including Orkney and Shetland, where cloud is expected to be well broken with only a small chance of a passing shower.

Parts of Northern Ireland, Wales, the Midlands and southern England will also have clear spells at times but there will be periods of cloudier weather and some splashes of rain.

In Northern Ireland, the Midlands and North Wales, the best chance of clear breaks will be earlier in the night.

Much of Scotland away from the far north, and northern England, will have limited opportunities. A few places may see the odd gap in the cloud but for most it will be cloudy and damp.

Andrew understands the pressure within A&E is huge but says the staff are absolutely fantastic

A patient spent more than two days waiting in an A&E department on two separate occasions - and says he will never go back.

Andrew Railton, 63, from Rhondda Cynon Taf, said he sat "on the same chair" for more than 50 hours on each visit after suffering first from pneumonia and then dangerously low potassium levels.

It comes as a £23m plan by the Welsh government promises to end A&E corridor care in Wales by 2029.

Senior emergency doctors have warned too many patients in Wales are experiencing "a terrible time" due to emergency care pressures and delays.

Railton attended the A&E department at Royal Glamorgan Hospital in Talbot Green, Rhondda Cynon Taf, after he developed pneumonia.

He said he was "pretty poorly" and sat in the waiting room for around nine hours before seeing a doctor.

"I was put in the chair and obviously put on the drip ... but basically sat in this draughty corridor," he said.

"They brought stools and chairs, and there were people basically just stood around all over the place with drips in them, and it was something Victorian. I was there for 50-odd hours."

A bed was eventually found for him and he stayed in hospital for a further three days.

But a few months later he was told to go to A&E again because of "deathly low" potassium levels.

"Believe it or not, I was put in exactly the same chair that I was in last time. And I sat in that chair overnight while I had a drip administered to me," he said.

Now Railton says there is "no chance in hell" of him going back to the A&E even if his "leg falls off."

Cwm Taf Morgannwg health board said it was sorry for Railton's experience and the distress caused.

The corridors in A&E are being used as places to care for patients

The Welsh government's new emergency care plan points to delays and problems in 2025-26:

Ambulances took an average of two hours and 24 minutes from arrival in hospital to transferring their patients, resulting in 184,850 "lost hours"

Patients aged 85 or over spent an average of seven hours and 13 minutes in A&E with 15% of all cases waiting more than 12 hours

62,346 people admitted as an emergency stayed more than 21 days in hospital

There are around 1,400 patients, at any given time, occupying beds that are clinically ready to leave

With each bed occupied costing £500-£600 a day, the bill to the NHS was £172m

Mabon ap Gwynfor says when someone needs emergency care, they should know help will come quickly

The new plan sets goals for the "whole journey" of the patient - from the scene of the emergency, through to recovery at home.

One of the key milestones is that A&E corridor care or care in other unsuitable spaces should be eliminated by 2029.

Mabon ap Gwynfor, Cabinet Minister for Health and Care, said: "When someone needs emergency care, they should know help will come quickly, they will receive the right care, and they will spend only as long in hospital as they need to.

"Too many people do not experience this consistently today and that must change."

Emergency doctors have frequently warned that patients too often face harm because they are being treated in unsafe spaces in A&E.

Speaking to Politics Wales, Dr Katja Empson, of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine, warned that too many patients were experiencing "terrible" conditions.

"They're often spending a very long time waiting for a bed, and often in a very inappropriate area," she said.

"We are causing harm because people are delayed in the emergency department."

The plan sets out an "ambition" to discharge patients from hospital, where possible, within 72 hours.

It includes making sure patients get early assessments from a senior clinicians, receive quick diagnostic tests and get rapid support from pharmacy and therapy and rehabilitation teams.

Planning for a safe transfer home should happen from the moment a patient arrives, the plan says.

The plan also aims to address relatively poor survival rates for people having cardiac arrests in communities.

It notes that of the 2,800 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occur each year - just one in 20 in Wales (5%) survive compared to 8% in England and 10% in Scotland.

There is an ambition for Wales to become a "nation of life-savers" by 2029 by training people to be more confident in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and raising awareness among children and young people.

New technology will be explored such as drones carrying defibrillators that can save lives.

Ed Grant says everyone should be taught CPR

The "nation of life-savers" aim is supported by Ed Grant, a Welsh Ambulance community first responder who was himself saved by CPR.

The 73-year-old from Barry spent 50 years volunteering in various emergency services.

"I'm actually living proof that CPR works," he said, recalling how his wife kept him alive after he suffered a cardiac arrest at home three years ago.

"Luckily my wife knows CPR because I taught her... she started CPR on me, called the ambulance and called one of my responders as well."

He said community responders can often reach patients first, particularly in rural areas.

"We work very much in tandem with the ambulance service... we can get there first and start dealing with it, keep the person alive and well until the ambulance can arrive," he said.

Dr Siobhan Lewis said as that hospital is not always the best place to be but is there if you need care around the clock

The plan will include new set of measures and targets which will be recorded and reported on annually from spring next year, with a review in 2030.

These will include measures of patient survival and recovery as well as people's experience of care including corridor care.

Dr Siobhan Lewis, National Clinical Lead for Frailty in NHS Wales and consultant geriatrician, said: "We are already seeing the effects of an ageing population and those living with multiple medical conditions in our acute care areas, and the need for person-centred care has never been greater."

Jesus Owono said he was experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel earlier this month

FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique says goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12-match suspension he received following his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.

Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel late on in the second-tier match between Andorra and Tenerife on 2 November.

De Miguel died the following day, aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's ban last week.

In a video posted on social media, Pique said players past and present, plus coaches and other goalkeepers, felt the incident was "an accident".

The former Spain and Barcelona defender added: "I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened."

Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision

Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban

The 12-match suspension was the maximum punishment Owono, 25, could have received, as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".

Following the decision, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera said he accepted the regulations do not specifically account for what happened, but acknowledged the ban "might feel light".

Pique also highlighted a recent on-field incident in Spain, when Albacete winger Jose Corpas accidentally kicked Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed in the head during a Spanish second division match.

Nigerian Liameed was knocked unconscious but was later discharged from hospital following medical checks, while Spaniard Corpas was shown a straight red card and handed a three-match ban.

"Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches," Pique said.

"With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?"

Owono has withdrawn from Equatorial Guinea's squad for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Zimbabwe this month, and Pique said it was unlikely he would return to action as soon as his suspension is served.

He added: "Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete.

"No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us."

Rwanda’s Foreign Affairs Minister Oliveir Nduhungirehe has lambasted his Congolese counterpart Wagner Kayikwamba for lying about what transpired behind closed doors during elections for the next La Francophonie Secretary General in Cambodia.

“DRC’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, who took part in closed-door meeting of Francophonie heads of state, should avoid lying to the public,” Nduhungirehe said early on Tuesday.

“She claims Louise Mushikiwabo was kept in office “on an interim basis” to “handle day-to-day affairs” and that her mandate is “exclusively intended to enable reform of the electoral process. This is blatant disinformation,” said Rwanda’s Chief diplomat.

He explains, “these words do not appear in the compromise initially proposed by Rwanda, negotiated with presidents of Senegal, Togo and Benin, and presented to President Tshisekedi, who reluctantly agreed to it.”

“Indeed, the DRC’s president wanted a short transition without Louise Mushikiwabo, but with the Administrator of the OIF, to handle day-to-day affairs and reform the electoral rules,” Nduhungirehe explains.

According to Nduhungirehe, Mushikiwabo’s mandate, “which runs until December 31, 2027, is therefore a full-fledged mandate with full authority to exercise it. And reforming the electoral process is one of its main objectives.”

“It should be made clear that it was Rwanda that, in its proposal, pledged not to put forward a candidate to succeed Mushikiwabo, which is common practice in international organizations. The DRC should therefore not try to take credit for it,” Nduhungirehe emphasized.

Venâncio Mondlane was the runner-up in the 2024 presidential election

Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.

Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.

Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.

Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.

Children shot dead after joining pot-banging protests in Mozambique

The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.

"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.

Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.

The demonstrations continued for months, with rights groups accusing security forces of using excessive force against protesters.

Amnesty International, citing local civil society organisations, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, which was one of the country's worst post-election crises since independence.

European Union election observers also reported irregularities in the October 2024 vote, raising questions about the credibility of the results.

Prosecutors accuse Mondlane of encouraging demonstrations that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security.

The charges include publicly glorifying criminal acts, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit crimes and offences linked to terrorism.

He could face up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge.

Mondlane has rejected the accusations, insisting that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency rather than encouraging violence.

His party, the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), has described the prosecution as politically motivated.

The Supreme Court has denied allegations of political interference in the proceedings.

A heavy deployment of police has been seen patrolling around the Supreme Court and major streets in Maputo ahead of the trial.

In a statement issued on Monday, Mozambique's police appealed to citizens to "preserve tolerance and peaceful coexistence," adding that the right to demonstrate must be exercised strictly within the limits of the law.

Police also pledged to protect people and property while acting preventively and proportionately in accordance with the rule of law.

The court has only granted access to selected media organisations, sparking criticism from journalists and press freedom campaigners.

Court officials say the restrictions are necessary because of limited seating capacity in the courtroom, but critics argue they undermine transparency in a case of significant public interest.

The proceedings are expected to be heard by five judges, with witnesses called by both the prosecution and defence.

Political observers warn that the trial could reignite tensions in a country still struggling to recover from the violence and deep political divisions that followed the 2024 elections.

Northern Ireland play Hungary in Budapest needing a point for Nations League promotion

With six of his starting outfield players against Ukraine on Saturday night having gone into the game a yellow card away from suspension, it was always likely that Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill would need to reshuffle his team for the Nations League Group B2 finale in Hungary.

That the player who picked up the booking ended up being Jamie Donley, however, has presented the boss with something of a selection conundrum.

The Tottenham Hotspur forward, currently on loan at Luton Town, has started the side's past 10 games at centre forward, a different role to the deeper position he has more usually occupied in his club career.

With O'Neill having circled through traditional number nine options such as Dion Charles, Jamie Reid and Lee Bonis since returning to the job four years ago, it feels as if Donley has made the shirt his own since being handed the start against Luxembourg 12 months ago.

While the manager has pushed back on the idea that Donley is playing out of position at international level, the one-game ban is certainly an untimely one with the former Leyton Orient and Oxford United loanee's hold-up play in particular against Ukraine showing how much he has grown into the role.

After the 21-year-old had a goal chalked off by the video assistant referee (VAR) on Saturday, he has still scored just once from open play for his country, but there is a growing appreciation that he is asked to bring much more than just goals to the team.

"He's been such a good player for us. Even without the goals, the way he holds the ball up and spreads the play, his movement is just so good. Playing balls in the air, he pins the defender so well," said Fulham midfielder Shea Charles.

"He's got better every game and he's like the perfect player for us."

There is no obvious like-for-like replacement in O'Neill's squad for a game in which they need a draw to secure promotion to Nations League A for the first time.

Arsenal's Ceadach O'Neill pulled out of the double-header through injury last week, with Josh Magennis, Callum Marshall and the uncapped pair of Eoin Kenny and Braiden Graham the other strikers in the travelling party.

Similar to the original ask of Donley, there is also an option to move a wide or deeper player such as Isaac Price into a central striking role.

With only three days between games, however, there has been little time to work on such a plan to replace a player whose four Spurs appearances all came under Ange Postecoglou in the 2023-24 season.

"There are other things we can do. We can change the shape a little bit, play with two front players," said O'Neill, who himself is suspended for the game after two bookings and will watch from the stands.

"There's a number of things that we will look at. Obviously the time between the games makes that somewhat more difficult in terms of preparation.

"We'll find hopefully the right player that can first of all fit into what we want to do, but obviously secondly give the opposition some problems as well."

Nobody in O'Neill's squad has more international caps or goals than Stevenage striker Magennis.

But while the 36-year-old has started 11 games in League One this season, it has been more than three years since he last did so at international level.

"My role has obviously changed since I've come into the squad," said the player with 94 international appearances and 12 goals to his name.

"If Michael wants to play with the target man and with experience, obviously, he's going to go for me. If he wants a like-for-like, he's probably going to go with Marshy [Callum Marshall]. So, me and Marshy will probably play rock, paper, scissors.

"Jamie brings so much to the team, but I don't think there's going to be a drastic downfall if one of us has to step in for us. I think the competition for places in the squad for us is absolutely brilliant and if you get that opportunity, you've just got to take it."

MN202611_vfa5e122sn.t:
Scotland slump to 4-0 defeat in Switzerland

As Zeki Amdouni arrowed in second-string Switzerland's fabulous fourth goal, the body language of dejected Scotland duo Andy Robertson and Ryan Christie was telling.

The captain's record-breaking 103rd cap played out in cruel fashion. Suited and booted for the occasion, with commemorative boots and a personalised armband, there was no cause for celebration as Robertson was, yet again, wheeled out afterwards to make sense of the 4-0 scudding in St Gallen.

So too were John McGinn and Kieran Tierney. Billy Gilmour, who has also surpassed the half-century caps landmark, also did a bit of talking. Substitute Christie was spared this time.

After a result of this kind, rounding up a humdrum maiden campaign for manager Sebastien Pocognoli, it's necessary for the experienced heads to front-up.

When he named his first squad, so much kudos was thrown the Belgian's way for breaking away from the norm and bleeding in the stars of tomorrow.

But such young and bright lights were only allowed to shine on the bench, at best, as Pocognoli turned to the tried and tested.

As former Scotland international Leanne Crichton said on BBC Scotland's Sportscene: "There's a reliance still, clearly, on that key core of Scotland players.

"And, when you listen to it post-match, they sound dejected, they don't sound that confident about what is going on. It is a difficult place to be."

Pocognoli's abject Scotland suffer 4-0 Nations League defeat in Switzerland

St Gallen was a mighty troubling place for the Scots on Monday night.

The calm, picturesque city was invaded by coral shirt and kilt-clad Scotsmen from Sunday, but they - and their heroes on the pitch - couldn't wait to get out of the place after a poor showing at the Sitterstadion.

A narrow half-time deficit turned into a drubbing on the final whistle, at which the Scots remained goalless despite a handful of hopeful situations.

McGinn, the scorer of Scotland's past three goals, directed a weak header goalbound before the break, while Scott McTominay - nearly one year on from his Hampden heroics against Denmark - missed a couple of glaring opportunities.

"If McTominay is not operating at his highest level for the national team, there is an impact on results," Crichton said.

"If McGinn doesn't produce the goods on an evening, we're in trouble.

"If Gilmour and Ferguson in the middle of the pitch [don't perform], if Christie doesn't come on with an impact, we are [too reliant].

"And that's where you need to breed a different confidence in a different group."

Kieron Bowie, who many hoped would be in from the off, came on just before the hour mark and got right in about it, as is the striker's style.

Winger Ben Gannon-Doak, dropped for Aaron Hickey, did come on after the wing-back ended up going off with an apparent hamstring injury before Kristi Montgomery was handed a debut with five minutes to go.

Wide-men Findlay Curtis and Josh McPake were left on the bench, again. Robbie Ure didn't make either matchday squad this camp.

All three natural wingers excite supporters, even if they have only been handed a matter of minutes, but Pocognoli's system does not suit them.

That said, the players insist they're invested in the project.

"We have to believe that we're going in the right direction," Robertson added after a beyond-deflating defeat.

"Of course, there's going to be humps in the road, but when I look back on Steve Clarke's opening six games - I can't remember all the results but - I don't think everyone was shouting and screaming about Steve Clarke's Scotland after the first six games.

"We're trying to get a team together and we're trying to build a good atmosphere off the pitch.

"People wanted change within the squad. We've done that change and now we need to try and integrate the squad.

"We need to get close as a squad again, integrate the young players, make them feel a part of it, make them step up - it's for us to try and help them do it."

Five European Union (EU) countries have announced plans to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, marking a significant shift in Europe’s migration policy and reviving a controversial arrangement previously pursued by the United Kingdom.

Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands unveiled the initiative on Monday, November 16, 2026, during a migration conference in Vienna, Austria, where officials from the five countries met with a Rwandan delegation led by Interior Minister Vincent Biruta.

The proposed facility, known as a return hub, will accommodate migrants whose asylum applications have been rejected in Europe and who have exhausted their legal avenues to remain in the EU but cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

The five governments hope to have the centre operational in 2027, with negotiations on the detailed arrangements expected to conclude in the coming months.

According to reports, the initial facility is expected to accommodate approximately 100 people, with each participating country potentially transferring around 20 migrants.

Unlike Britain’s previous arrangement with Kigali, the new initiative is expected to operate as an open reception facility rather than a detention centre.

Those transferred would be granted residence rights and access to healthcare, education and employment opportunities, allowing them to integrate into Rwandan society.

Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the initiative would provide a second opportunity for people who no longer have the legal right to remain in their European host countries.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who attended the Vienna announcement alongside Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, described the initiative as a major shift in European migration management.

She argued that the arrangement would help European governments regain control of their borders and discourage irregular migration.

Although the five European countries have agreed to cover the costs of transferring and accommodating migrants in Rwanda, they have not yet disclosed the financial value of the proposed arrangement.

The European governments are expected to finance relocation, temporary accommodation and integration services.

However, the amount Rwanda will receive, if any, has not been publicly established.

The initiative has also brought renewed attention to the previous migration agreement between Rwanda and the United Kingdom, which was eventually abandoned.

Under the UK’s Migration and Economic Development Partnership, signed in April 2022, the British government committed to paying Rwanda £370 million (approximately $470 million at the time) in fixed development-related payments.

The arrangement also included an additional £120 million once 300 migrants had been transferred, alongside £20,000 for every relocated individual and up to £150,874 per person to cover asylum processing and integration costs over five years.

According to the UK’s National Audit Office, the financial commitments under the arrangement were substantially higher than the initial £370 million headline figure.

By the time the partnership was terminated in 2024, the British government had paid Rwanda £290 million.

Meanwhile, total UK Home Office expenditure associated with the partnership and its implementation had reached approximately £715 million by June 2024.

Despite the substantial expenditure, Britain did not transfer any asylum seekers to Rwanda under the scheme, although four people volunteered to relocate.

The new European initiative is different because it targets people whose asylum applications have already been rejected and who have exhausted their legal appeals, rather than transferring people to another country while their asylum claims are being processed.

The proposed arrangement has already attracted criticism from human rights organisations, which question whether transferring migrants to a third country provides sufficient protection for their fundamental rights.

Critics argue that sending people to countries with which they have no previous connection could expose them to legal uncertainty and weaken accountability for their treatment.

The United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, has stressed that any such arrangements must comply with international refugee and human rights law.

However, the participating governments maintain that the initiative will operate within European and international legal frameworks, with safeguards to protect those transferred.

The European Union’s new Returns Regulation, approved in October 2026, provides a legal framework allowing member states to establish return hubs outside the bloc, subject to human rights protections and other international legal obligations.

The regulation excludes unaccompanied minors from such arrangements.

The announcement places Rwanda at the centre of a new European approach to migration management, as governments increasingly explore partnerships with countries outside Europe to facilitate the return of migrants who have no legal right to remain within the bloc.

Ishirahamwe mpuzamakungu riharanira agateka ka zina muntu, Human Rights Watch (HRW), ryaneguye umugambi w'ibihugu bitanu vyo mw'ishirahamwe ry'Ubumwe bwa Buraya (EU/UE) wo kurungika mu Rwanda abantu basavye ubuhungiro ariko ntibaburonke muri ivyo bihugu, rivuga ko ari "ukwitandukanya kubabaje" n'indangagaciro uwo muryango wubakiyeko.

Ku wa mbere, Autriche, Danemark, Ubudagi, Ubugiriki n'Ubuholandi vyemeje ko hariko haraba ibiganiro kuri uwo mugambi. Hari inyuma y'inama yerekeye ikibazo c'abimukira yabereye i Vienne muri Autriche.

Bitegekanijwe ko abo bimukira batangura kurungikwa mu Rwanda mu mwaka uza wa 2027.

HRW ivuga ko uwo mugambi ushobora gushira mu kaga agateka k'abo bantu kuko, ku bwayo, Urwanda rutubahiriza agateka ka muntu. HRW yongerako ko ruhasha canke rugacecekesha abanegura ubutegetsi bwarwo, harimwo abaharanira uburenganzira bwa muntu.

BBC Gahuzamiryango yashatse kumenya ico reta y'Urwanda ivuga kuri ibi birego vya HRW, n'uko Umushikiranganji w'imigenderanire, Olivier Nduhungirehe, avuga ko atigera yishura ku bivugwa n'iryo shirahamwe kuko abona ko iryo shirahamwe ari "iteshagaciro ry'uburenganzira bwa muntu".

Umushikiranganji w'umutekano, Vincent Biruta, ni we yari yaserukiye Urwanda mu biganiro vy'i Vienne. Yavuze ko igihugu ciwe ciyemeje gukorana n'ibihugu bifatanyabikorwa vyo ku mugabane wa Buraya mu gutanga "umuti utekanye, wemewe n'amategeko kandi w'iteka n'icubahiro ku bimukira".

Yavuze ko Urwanda ruzokorana n'ivyo bihugu mu "gukosora ubusumbasumbane bwigaragaza kw'isi mu bijanye n'amahirwe yo gushikira iterambere ry'ubutunzi", abona ko ari yo "mvo nyamukuru ituma haba ubwimukira butubahirije amategeko".

Mw'itangazo ryasohoye , ishirahamwe HRW riragaragaza ingorane zishobora gushikira abo bimukira harimwo gupfungwa agasakisaki, gufatwa nabi canke gusubizwa mu bihugu baje bavamwo, aho bashobora guhura n'ingorane.

Rivuga kandi ko uwo mugambi udahuye n'amategeko mashasha agenga Ubumwe bwa Buraya mu bijanye no gusubiza abimukira mu bihugu vyabo.

Ku bwa HRW, ayo mategeko ategekanya ko amasezerano nk'ayo – yabaye hagati y'Urwanda n'ibihugu bitanu vya Buraya – uwo muryango ukwiye kuyagirana n'ibihugu vyubahiriza amategeko mpuzamakungu akingira agateka ka zina muntu.

HRW isaba ivyo bihugu guhagarika uwo mugambi kuko isanga ushobora kwongerereza Urwanda amafaranga n'ubushobozi mu bijanye no guhonyanga agateka ka zina muntu. Ni mu gihe kandi, nk'uko HRW ibandanya ibivuga, igisirikare c'ico gihugu cagirizwa gufasha umuhari M23 – ubu wahindutse FRN – urwanira mu buseruko bwa Repuburika ya Demokarasi ya Kongo (RDC). Urwanda rurabihakana.

HRW mu kurangiza yibutsa ko muri Nzero (1) uwu mwaka, Ubudagi, Ubugiriki, Danmark n'Ubuholande vyari vyagaragaje amakenga bifise ku kuntu ibintu vyifashe mu Rwanda, igihe ico gihugu cariko kirasuzumwa n'ishirahamwe mpuzamakungu ONU ku bijanye n'agateka ka zina muntu.

Imbere y'uko uwo mugambi utangura icese, abaserukira ibihugu biwurimwo babwiye itororokanirizo ry'amakuru AFP ko hazobanza kuba igerageza, ikigo kibijejwe kibanze kirungikirwe abimukira 100.

Ni ukuvuga ko kimwe cose muri vyo gishobora kurungika abimukira 20.

Mu mwaka wa 2023, sentare nkuru y'Ubwongereza yanzuye ko umugambi w'ico gihugu wo kurungika mu Rwanda abimukira uteye kubiri n'amategeko. Mu nyuma, wahavuye ukurwaho n'ubutegetsi bushasha bw'Ubwongereza.

Fernando Alonso will take on the Dakar Rally for a second time

Two-time Formula 1 world champion Fernando Alonso will lead Aston Martin's attempt to win the Dakar Rally in January 2027.

The 45-year-old Spaniard, who drives for the British team in Formula 1, previously contested the prestigious rally raid event in 2020 for Toyota.

Aston Martin have struggled in the first year of F1's new regulations in the Adrian Newey-designed AMR26 car.

Alonso sits 17th in the drivers' championship, team-mate Lance Stroll 22nd, and the team 10th in the constructors', only ahead of last-placed Cadillac.

Alonso, who recently signed a new Aston Martin deal and is widely regarded as one of the biggest talents in motorsport history, is joined in the Dreadnought by co-driver Marc Coma.

Coma is a five-time winner of the Dakar on a motorbike and was also Alonso’s co-driver in 2020.

The two other cars will be driven by nine-time world rally champion Sebastien Loeb of France and current world rally raid champion Lucas Moraes of Brazil.

"After deciding to continue racing in Formula 1 with Aston Martin, I thought carefully about Dakar," said Alonso. "In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely.

"I have enormous respect for this race and the specialists who have mastered it. Having Marc alongside me again is very important, and with Aston Martin, Prodrive, Sebastien and Lucas we have an exceptional team."

It will be Aston's first involvement in the famously gruelling and dangerous race and they will go up against more established Dakar teams such as Toyota and KTM.

Aston's Dakar machines will be prepared by Prodrive - who had considerable success in rallying with Subaru in the 1990s and 2000s.

Despite challenges on the tarmac in F1, Aston have enjoyed much-improved performances in the World Endurance Championship this year, including at the season finale at Monza last month through the 007 Valkyrie car driven by Tom Gamble and Harry Tincknell.

Alonso could even drive the Valkyrie at the famous Le Mans 24 Hours in 2027 - F1 commitments permitting - where he won with Toyota in 2018 and 2019.

Alonso came 13th at the Dakar Rally in 2020 for Toyota

Aston Martin have not had much luck during 2026 in F1, but have had a much-improved second season in the Word Endurance Championship with the Valkyrie hypercar - one Aston that Alonso is yet to compete in...

The Spaniard has had success in a sportscar, though, winning Le Mans in 2018 and 2019 with Toyota

And for Cadillac at the Daytona 24 Hours in the same year

Success at the Indy 500, however, has so far eluded him

The 2027 Dakar Rally will begin in Portugal on 9 January and after 12 stages end in Morocco on 23 January.

Last month it was announced Dakar would be switched from Saudi Arabia following the unrest in the Middle East because of the Iran war.

The race, which also includes other classifications of cars, as well as lorries and motorbikes, was traditionally held between Paris and Dakar from the late 1970s, but the route has been adjusted over the years for promotional and safety reasons.

Alonso's previous Dakar brought a 13th-place finish. A couple of crashes caused by inexperience of the event delayed him, but a second-place finish on one stage showed his pace and potential.

"Formula 1 remains my priority," he said. "But I am a racing driver, and challenges like this are why I love competing. I'm looking forward to seeing what we can achieve."

The 20th La Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh ended after a marathon of side events from November 15, leading to a meeting of the organisation’s heads of State and government on 16th.

Themed, “Reinvesting in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability,” the heads of state and government of the Francophonie adopted three texts.

The Phnom Penh Declaration includes; Resolution on Crisis Situations, Peacebuilding and Phnom Penh Appeal for the Protection of Cultural Heritage.

Cambodia now holds the presidency of the Summit, which has also admitted Saint Kitts and Nevis and Manitoba as observer members.

The Phnom Penh Declaration reaffirms the support of States and governments for the OIF’s work in promoting the rule of law, mediation, and support for transitions, and places young people and women at the heart of peacebuilding.

It calls for defending a reliable information space against manipulation and interference, keeping humans at the center of artificial intelligence, and strengthening the Francophone voice in global digital governance, particularly in view of the Geneva Summit on AI in 2027.

The Resolution reviews nearly twenty situations, from Armenia to Sudan, including Haiti, the Sahel, and the Middle East.

It expresses, in particular, the concern of the Heads of State and Government regarding the border tensions between Cambodia and Thailand and the situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, and welcomes the fact-finding mission deployed by the Secretary-General in response to the DRC’s appeal for solidarity from the Francophonie.

In the land of Angkor, the Phnom Penh Appeal finally commits states and governments to better protect cultural heritage, to fight against the illicit trafficking of cultural property and to promote its restitution.

In the absence of a consensus on the choice of a candidate or the holding of a vote, the heads of state and government accepted the proposal of the Cambodian presidency of the Summit to extend the mandate of the Secretary-General, Louise Mushikiwabo, by twelve months, in order to allow for an election to be held in 2027.

During this period, states and governments will have the opportunity to propose amendments to the electoral procedure in effect since 2022 to the Secretary-General.

At the closing ceremony, the Secretary General recalled the reforms undertaken since 2019 to create a more transparent, efficient, and visible organization.

She stated that she respected the collective decision of the Heads of State and Government and that she was carrying out her assigned mission solely in the interest of the organization, while urging the Francophonie to commit resolutely to addressing the challenges of artificial intelligence.

The 21st Summit will be held in Ottawa, Canada, preceded by a pre-summit for Francophone youth in New Brunswick.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has framed the summit around the discoverability of Francophone content in the age of artificial intelligence.

The OIF has 92 states and governments: 53 members, 5 associate members and 34 observers.

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft were "completely unacceptable"

Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.

South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.

These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.

The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".

The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.

Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.

South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.

It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.

The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.

Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.

Tensions are flaring between Japan and Russia, which are locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean.

For months, Moscow has been ratcheting up the pressure on Tokyo.

In August, Putin paid his first visit to one of these islands, prompting sharp rebuke from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In October, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, Grindr, has defended its $120 (£91) per month premium subscription service, which launches globally today.

Edge offers AI-powered services such as daily personalised profile recommendations that aim to provide better matches and limit scrolling.

The company's CEO, George Arison, told BBC News it would be a "very different Grindr experience" which was aimed at a "small community of users" - and was unapologetic about its cost.

"I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not," he said.

Grindr has long had a free service, and offers two additional tiers that cost between $22.99 and $44.99 per month.

There was a mixed reaction from users BBC News spoke to in San Francisco to the new, much more expensive version of the app.

"The current premium Grindr tier is already really expensive," said a user named Rybin, who told the BBC the company's newest offering "just seems really out of touch with the community."

"I think that that's really disheartening, and it kind of leaves a bad taste in my mouth," said another user, Adrian.

"The cost doesn't bother me," said a user named Michael. "All of these apps have premium tiers so saying that Grindr shouldn't have that when like it exists across all these other apps used for connection doesn't make sense."

He noted that high-end dating apps like The League can charge much more.

Grindr has been experimenting with Edge for much of the last year in markets including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.

On its earnings call earlier this month, the company said almost 400,000 users had registered for the service in the first 72 hours that it was available for testing.

Inside Grindr, Edge is viewed as a way to drive future growth in an industry has struggled in recent years.

For those who can afford it, the service promises to offer insights about a user's compatibility with prospective matches. It also resurfaces a user's past connections alongside summaries of previous interactions.

The current $120 monthly fee comes after the company tested charging hundreds of dollars more than that. And Arison has left open the possibility of increasing the cost in the future.

Arison told the BBC he's not concerned that intoducing an ultra-premium offering will pit "haves" against "have-nots" on the social networking platform.

Edge users "being willing to pay more for that set of features will result in us being able to subsidise the product for everybody else," Arison said.

"It's a choice that people make on whether they want to be on it."

The use of AI to develop the Edge service is part of Grindr's attempt to become what it calls an "AI-first company."

Arison said the company was investing in AI to ensure it can build products more quickly and cheaply.

In September, as the debate over AI safety raged throughout Silicon Valley, Arison told the BBC that his concerns about what he called an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic" had prompted him to instruct some of his engineers to stop using Anthropic's technology.

Anthropic is due to start selling shares to the public for the first time this week.

Although Anthropic's Claude Code tool remain in use at Grindr now, Arison said the company is on track to completely phase it out of his company's workflows by next year.

He said Grindr was once a very heavy user of Claude Code but that it was no longer the primary tool the use to write code.

"Anthropic's built an amazing amazing set of products, and they should be very proud of what they've done," Arison said. "They should aim to win with the awesome products they have, rather than regulatory capture that they're trying to win with, oftentimes."

Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.

This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".

US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.

But with 97% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.

BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.

The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.

This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.

Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state

Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.

A New York Times story , external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.

Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.

President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".

But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.

"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.

Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot

Senator Sullivan was joined by President Trump at a campaign rally ahead of the vote

Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.

"There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.

On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:

- Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent

There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.

A sample ballot for the US Senate election in Alaska

As of Monday, Peltola holds 49.94% of the vote.

In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.

Democrat Mary Peltola's said on Saturday she will "decisively be elected" as Alaska's next senator

Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.

Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".

Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.

We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.

A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.

"The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."

Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May

As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.

On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.

South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , external , a US-based think-tank.

China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.

Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.

These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.

But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.

The BBC has contacted Singapore, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms. Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".

The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.

Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.

Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.

"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.

Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.

The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.

But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.

That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

Blackburn Rovers head coach Tony Mowbray has stepped back from his role with the Championship club due to health issues.

The 62-year-old returned for a second spell in June having previously spent five years managing Rovers between 2017 and 2022.

Mowbray had previously stepped away from the game during his time as Birmingham City boss in early 2024 following a health scare, and later revealed he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer.

"I'm immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I've loved working with them," Mowbray said in a statement.

"Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you've given me. It's been a pleasure working alongside you.

"To the fans, thank you for the way you've supported me and the team this season. I've always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me."

Mowbray has transformed Blackburn this season, after a they hovered around the relegation places for much of last term before eventually finishing 20th in the Championship and five points above the drop zone.

They are currently 13th in the Championship table having won six of their 15 league games and three points outside the play-offs.

Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Russell Brand in 2023, which he denies

A woman who has made allegations against Russell Brand has said she finds it "upsetting" and "really shocking" that he was able to claim he was innocent from prison , following his conviction for rape and sexual assault.

Speaking after the comedian's wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, Mia Latter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she found it "appalling" to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she said.

Latter, 37, who has alleged she was raped by Brand when she was 16, was one of six women who spoke out against the comedian in a 2023 documentary. None of the women were complainants in his recent criminal trial and Brand denies their claims.

Brand is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being found guilty at Southwark Crown Court.

In recent years he has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following, including in the US. In the message read out by his wife on their show, Brand said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

Latter said the broadcast "was really shocking to me... it was appalling, frankly, it was upsetting to watch".

She said the woman who gave evidence in the trial "got their verdict, and for him to say, 'I'm innocent, I'm not guilty' - well, you are, you're a convicted rapist now. There's no arguing with that".

Downing Street said on Monday it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said that "prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims".

Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time and originally made allegations against him as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation in 2023.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, Latter said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.

She has waived her right to anonymity in order to campaign for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in the UK that would make sexual relationships between 16 and 17 year-olds and adults illegal.

Latter told the Sunday Times the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings. She told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.

Latter told Today a staggered age of consent could have stopped her relationship with Brand "dead in its tracks".

She said: "It would have 100% made a difference because my parents tried to stop the relationship.

"They tried to prevent me from seeing him... But if it had been a criminal offence for him to be having a relationship with me, none of the subsequent abuse would have ever happened because they would have been able to stop the relationship dead in its tracks."

Latter also told Today that she and the complainants in Brand's trial had been accused of being "money hungry".

She said she had initially been reluctant to speak out because "I knew that the audience that he'd cultivated over the past few years would come for me".

"It's a criminal trial, there's no money.

"Me talking to the Times, me talking to you, me doing any interviews, there's no money, there's not a penny. We're just doing this in the pursuit of justice."

But Latter said Brand had been "monetising all these platforms" during his trial by continuing to make videos that appeared with advertisements on social media.

DRC’s Juliana Lumumba may have been thrown into the battle for Secretary General seat of La Francophonie organisation without her interest, and later her candidature humiliatingly withdrawn without her knowledge, it has emerged.

Taarifa Investigative Desk has established from Kinshasa’s diplomatic sources that last year Lumumba had declined to run for OIF Secretary General office.

However, the Kinshasa establishment insisted that she gets into the race and was promised enormous resources for campaigns.

As the campaign heat mounted between Kigali and Kinshasa, it emerged that Lumumba was lacking resources to mobilise yet government had promised to pour in millions of Congolese francs.

Just two days before the elections, Kinshasa government through a statement by the foreign affairs ministry announced that it had withdrawn Lumumba’s candidature.

Kinshasa argued it had chosen to align with a European candidate Dacian Cioloș, a former Prime Minister of Romania.

Insiders say that Kinshasa regime political calculators had allegedly sensed that Lumumba was no match for rival Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda.

However, in the statement announcing Lumumba’s withdrawal from the race, Kinshasa argued, “the decision did not reflect any doubts about Lumumba’s abilities, experience or commitment to advocating for reforms within the OIF.”

Lumumba according to sources close to her said that she was equally surprised and felt she was used and humiliated.

It has emerged that Lumumba was sidelined and not consulted or informed before withdrawing her candidature.

Like many others, Lumumba found out from social media that Kinshasa government had discontinued her from the race for Secretary General of OIF.

The statement on DRC’s candidature withdrawal was hastly removed from the foreign affairs ministry portal and replaced by another.

“She reportedly saw this way of handling things as a sign of disrespect toward her,” a source said under condition of anonymity.

Mauricio Pochettino says he would tell Pep Guardiola to take the United States job if the former Manchester City manager was offered it.

Pochettino, 54, is leaving his role as the US men's team head coach to become Manchester United 's new manager from 18 November, after signing a two-and-a-half-year contract until June 2029.

He takes charge of his final game with the US on Tuesday when they face Haiti in the second leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals in Cincinnati, Ohio.

Guardiola, 55, is taking a one-year sabbatical after stepping down as City boss in May.

Reports have suggested Guardiola could be a contender to succeed Pochettino in the US, although there has been no formal contact between the Spaniard and the United States Soccer Federation.

Pochettino told reporters on Monday his advice to Guardiola would be to take the role, "because it's a perfect moment to arrive at the federation."

The Argentine added: "Everything is on the right path, in the right direction.

"Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people - the players can fit his style."

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino is replacing Michael Carrick at United. Carrick was sacked as head coach last week with the club in the relegation zone in 18th place.

His long-time assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeping coach Toni Jimenez and athletic coach, 31-year-old son Sebastiano Pochettino, arrived in England following the US's 6-0 first-leg victory over Haiti in Miami last weekend.

Pochettino's first test back in the Premier League is an away trip to Anfield to face fourth-placed Liverpool on Sunday.

"They are in advance, they are preparing all there, because Wednesday when we will arrive, it is going to be non-stop," he said.

The contaminated Mobuoy dump is thought to cover more than 100 acres of land

More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.

The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.

Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.

Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.

Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".

He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.

Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.

Andrew Muir says it could take a generation to clean up the Mobuoy dump in County Londonderry

Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.

The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.

The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.

"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .

The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.

"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."

The site, located on the outskirts of the city, is a former recycling plant

Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.

"I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said.

"I am pushing ahead with real enthusiasm with this."

Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site.

Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it.

One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.
