MN202611_1d5ps2xiojr.t:
The attack on Bilkis Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots

The article has details that some readers may find disturbing

A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.

Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back.

The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.

All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage . In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order .

In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.

The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".

On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken".

"She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary."

The riots began after a fire on a passenger train in Godhra town killed 60 Hindu pilgrims

Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".

The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.

Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.

When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child.

They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she'd told me in 2017 . Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.

How a Gujarat riot victim stood up to her rapists

India Supreme Court cancels release of 2002 riots rapists

India PM Modi's government okayed rapists' release

Her attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.

Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.

Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.

The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims

Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.

In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief".

"I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said.

"For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again."

Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives".

"I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."

Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.

In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

“Starting in 2027, the Carester-Malaco project will enable rare earths to be processed in Malaysia, with refining capacity in France,” President Macron said Tuesday.

So You Are competing in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington Racecourse on 3 November

The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.

In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.

Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".

Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.

"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."

So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.

The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.

The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said.

"So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.

Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.

In a statement, REC Equine Specialists - the hospital where the horse died - said a contractor had been hired to dispose of the So You Are's body.

"We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that."

"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally."

The company added that it had stopped using the contractor, and was reviewing its processes to make sure they known exactly how horses are handled after leaving their hospital.

"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again."

Jowett's video appeared to be filmed at a public rubbish drop-off and land facility called Lucas Heights, in Sutherland Shire, south of Sydney.

The waste management company that runs the landfill site said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported.

MN202611_zv4292vzno.t:
Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time

Uefa has finally identified a candidate to take on Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

Less than 48 hours before Wednesday night's deadline, European football's governing body announced that French Football Federation (FFF) president Philippe Diallo had received the unanimous support of its executive committee.

A late surprise choice, Uefa claimed it had "full confidence in [him] to provide the leadership needed."

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it seeks to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football were known to have hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he had the credibility and unifying potential to be able to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is not afraid to stand up to Infantino.

In September, he claimed the Fifa president had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister says Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, there are hopes at Uefa that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy significant support in parts of Africa and beyond.

There remains uncertainty over precisely how many of Uefa's full 55-strong membership will back Diallo, and some senior officials at leading European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."

Some also believe that a non-European candidate would have a much greater chance of unifying opposition against Infantino.

But McAllister remains optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different when the heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered some setbacks.

Uefa called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, and then potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stand for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by £2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"As I've said all along, this is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch. Whoever wins the presidential election next year, that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

So far, the legal action has not appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means the spotlight could intensify in other ways too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with US President Donald Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said Infantino and FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But now, armed with extra powers, they could force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Under mounting pressure , Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Although they will have to travel to its Zurich base to do so, and access will be under "strict protocols", Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election.

Recent months have seen a series of damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

Could Infantino even be ruled ineligible to stand? According to Portuguese lawyer Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - Infantino should not be allowed to be a candidate in the election as Fifa rules limit presidents to three terms. In 2022, Fifa's Council agreed that his first period in office - between 2016 and 2019 - should not count as he was effectively completing the remainder of Blatter's term after his resignation. But as Maduro has said, a national association or confederation would need to challenge this decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

Japan Football Association honorary president, Kozo Tashima, has announced his intention to stand , along with former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega. But with uncertainty over how much support either man will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris , external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.

Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.

Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.

Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.

Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024

Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.

Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China

In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".

They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

The Moon sculpture is hanging at the St Helier Methodist Centre

People visiting a large illuminated sculpture of the Moon have said it is an "amazing" sight.

ArtHouse Jersey has brought Luke Jerram's artwork to the St Helier Methodist Centre until Sunday 29 November.

The 6m (20ft) wide display, which has been shown around the world, features detailed imagery of the lunar surface from photographs by Nasa.

Arthouse CEO Tom Dingle said: "Something that makes the most of a public space, that makes us think about the world around us, about ourselves, but also something that we can all share together all at once, is really exciting."

Eva, nine, said it was "cool" to see a sculpture of the Moon up close

The Moon follows a similar public artwork display in Jersey in 2023, when more than 31,000 people visited the Floating Earth on Queen's Valley Reservoir .

The installation features light and sound displays, which ArtHouse said would allow people "to encounter our closest celestial neighbour in an entirely new way".

Nine-year-old Ava thought the moon was "cool" and "like a big spot in the middle of the sky".

Primrose Keenan also enjoyed the exhibit, saying it was "amazing".

"We saw the Earth on the lake as well a few couple of years ago and that was amazing too," she added.

Toby Balderson said: "It does make a difference being able to see everything in such detail.

"We always just see little snapshots of it."

Youngsters Aquila and Starla, who are sisters, said it looked "really good" and "very big".

Dingle added: "Sometimes to stop, to take a pause and to reflect on the wider things, to think about the world out there, is actually really healthy and therapeutic."

He said the exhibit also showed the importance of free public artwork: "It enlivens our public realm, it gives us something to do together.

"It actually can change the pace for a day. It can give somebody a moment to reflect and it can mean something different to everybody - and yet we have the same universal experience at the same time."

The government says it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.

But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.

A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.

The £330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.

The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.

The Liberal Democrats said the deal was "dangerous".

There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used .

Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.

Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".

The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.

The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.

Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".

"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.

Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".

Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.

Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

Police cordoned off the area where the shooting happened

A Costa Rican journalist who denounced alleged links between politicians and drug traffickers in the Central American country has been shot dead.

Police said gunmen on a motorbike ambushed Camilo Rodríguez, 50, as he was travelling in his car north of the capital, San José, on Monday afternoon.

The independent reporter earlier said he had been receiving death threats from drug trafficking gangs.

Local media reported that it was the first murder of a journalist in more than two decades in Costa Rica. It comes at a time when transnational crime gangs are increasing their presence in the country, driving up its formerly low homicide rate.

The president of the Costa Rican Journalists' Association, Yanancy Noguera, said that "all evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica - a person who published information about organised crime in the country".

Rodríguez had been working as a journalist for several decades, both in radio and in print.

Most recently, he had been uploading videos to social media in which he named public figures such as judges, business people and politicians, which he alleged were corrupt or had ties to known drug traffickers.

In one of his videos, he alleged that the home of Costa Rica's President, Laura Fernández, had been constructed by a company that he said had links to a criminal gang.

Fernández, who categorically denied any wrongdoing, took the journalist to court, accusing him of defamation.

Reacting to his murder in a video message, the president strongly condemned the attack, calling it "a stain on freedom of expression".

She added that she had instructed police to do their utmost to "punish Camilo's murderers".

Rodríguez had also tried to stand for political office, seeking to run as the presidential candidate for the Costa Rican Renovation Party in 2021.

However, his candidacy was rejected by the electoral authorities after the party failed to meet the necessary criteria required to file candidates.

Costa Rica's Attorney General, Carlo Díaz, said that "silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society".

MN202611_1obx131oyhn.t:
Diego Gomez's shot against Crystal Palace soars over Walter Benitez

David Beckham's goal from the halfway line against Wimbledon in 1996 is one of football's iconic moments.

It helped to catapult the Manchester United midfielder to global stardom and remains a staple of highlight reels.

The impudence to shoot from such a distance highlighted the exceptional talent and character of the future England captain.

Premier League players are now trying their luck from long range more regularly, testing their instinct, precision and technique.

Diego Gomez's stunning 51-metre (56-yard) strike for Brighton against Crystal Palace last month added to the spectacular list in the Premier League, while players in the EFL and FA Cup have contributed their own.

There have already been 19 attempts from over 50 metres this season, on course to beat last season's Premier League total of 26.

Of the 2,733 shots in the Premier League this term, 0.7% of them have come from over halfway - up on 0.3% over the course of last season.

This sample size is admittedly small. And in the case of goals scored from distance lower down the football pyramid, this is data that isn't readily available.

But why are we seeing a growing number of shots being taken from such extravagant distance?

Gomez tried to score from deep in his own half during Brighton 's 2-0 win at Sunderland on 10 October.

A week later, he beat Walter Benitez with the longest-range goal in the Premier League since Wayne Rooney's 57.6m strike for Everton against West Ham in 2017.

The Paraguayan took advice from Lionel Messi, when the pair were at Inter Miami, to always look to play the ball forward to another level.

It is not just Premier League players who are trying their luck from outrageous distances.

Charlie McNeill scored from halfway for Crewe in their recent 2-1 FA Cup win against AFC Wimbledon.

The on-loan Sheffield Wednesday forward, who played once for Manchester United before leaving Old Trafford in 2024, beat goalkeeper Joe Bursik to open the scoring.

Having done it while at Manchester City and Manchester United 's academies, the 23-year-old felt his latest attempt was instinctive.

He told BBC Sport: "Goalies nowadays are always quite high up the pitch - playing a sweeper-keeper role - and I always have a thought if I ever got into that situation to have a go.

"You see it more and more. I had the opportunity so I thought: 'Why not have a go?'

"It was one of those goals. I turned and saw him off his line and in that split-second made the decision to shoot.

"I knew I caught it sweetly and I was following it the whole way in so I knew it had a good chance, but as the keeper was going back I thought he was going to get it.

"When I watched it back it dropped quite early, but as it was getting closer and closer I thought it was going to go over because it went quite high but it dropped in."

Crewe Alexandra's Charlie McNeill talking about the rise in halfway line goals

McNeill joins a growing number of players to have scored from the halfway line or inside their own half over the past 18 months.

Preston Fearon, now on loan at Forest Green, scored two goals from around the halfway line for West Ham Under-21s in their win against Burnley last month.

Gbemi Arubi was barely a stride over the halfway line when he scored for Burton against Peterborough in October.

Last season, Abdul Fatawu (Leicester), Ryan Ledson (Huddersfield), Reyes Cleary (Barnsley), Regan Hendry (Mansfield) and Sammy Braybrooke (Newport) all scored from the halfway line or inside their own half in the EFL.

Two years ago, Chelsea 's Moises Caicedo scored from the centre circle against Bournemouth.

So what is sparking this apparent trend?

Is it all about the goalkeeper's position, as they stand higher up the pitch to either stop opposition attacks or get their own team moving?

"You've got to execute it properly, but it plays a big part. Most keepers are like that, high out the net, because we are playing over the top so they are there first, to get the ball," said McNeill.

"I have always had it in my head and have tried it a couple of times. Although it's not like I do my homework and see he is always off his line. It's one of those instinctive moments."

Paul Robinson scored two goals in his career, one for Tottenham and one for Leeds

Asmir Begovic holds the record for the longest-range Premier League goal when the goalkeeper scored from 95.7m for Stoke against Southampton in 2013.

Two other goalkeepers have scored from their own half: Tim Howard for Everton against Bolton in 2012 and Paul Robinson, who netted for Tottenham against Watford in 2007.

Yet they were flukes rather than by design - similar to Barrow goalkeeper Ben Winterbottom's goal from his own half in their 3-0 National League win at Gateshead on Saturday.

Robinson, who also scored for Leeds against Swindon in 2004 , external , feels conceding from distance is now a risk managers are willing to take.

The former England international said: "We've seen the game evolve in the way where the goalkeeper becomes a key figure in starting a pattern of play. The manager wants the goalkeeper at the base of the back three, four or five.

"But then also we're seeing a lot more teams playing with a higher line and the goalkeeper then has to take a higher line of starting position to read the through ball.

"When your team are playing a high line, you obviously have to be further up the field and you're concentrating on where your defensive line is, as opposed to where the football is at times.

"It's one of those things modern-day managers are willing to accept if and when it does happen, because of the way they want their goalkeeper to play.

"We see so many managers come out now and say: 'It's OK. I'm quite happy with them making mistakes. This is the way I want them to play. Blame me because that's what I've asked them to do.'

"We're probably entering that type of territory with it."

With attackers aware of the higher starting position of opposing keepers - a result of teams pressing high - and likely to have been encouraged by the success of other long-range efforts across football, attempts from extreme distance are becoming more frequent in the Premier League this season.

The conversion of efforts from more than 50 metres have increased too - up to 5.3% this season, compared to 1.1% across the previous three seasons combined, with Gomez's strike the first Premier League goal scored from over 50 metres since the 2023-24 season.

It's a small sample size, so more time is required for clearer trends, at least in the Premier League to be established.

But with more long shots being taken and keepers starting higher, there is a suggestion (and hope) we may see more Goal of the Season contenders before the term is out.

MN202611_5aaz86acy.t:
"It's almost impossible not to qualify."

The statement is enough to make any Scotland fan uncomfortable, but that's been the relaxed theme going into this Nations League campaign among some outside of Hampden.

Euro 2028 has various different access routes, especially for the host nations of England, Republic of Ireland, Scotland and Wales, who even have two spare spaces between them secured before a ball is kicked.

But, in the bleak, barren and grim aftermath of Scotland's 4-0 scudding by Switzerland in St Gallen, "almost impossible" almost feels like a challenge.

Scotland began with three shots at reaching the finals, where they would play at Hampden Park if they made it. We're now down to two.

They could have qualified for the Euro 2028 finals with help from the Nations League. Not straightforward, but absolutely achievable.

Finish top of group B1 containing Switzerland, Slovenia and North Macedonia, then prevail in the play-off.

In Sebastien Pocognoli's first six games in charge, he failed to deliver that, his new-look squad and system only offering seven points.

Not only that but that third-place finish has further repercussions.

Scotland's next route lies in the Euro qualifiers, with the draw taking place in Belfast on 6 December. Can't wait.

Pocognoli's team will go into pot three for that, making a shot at progression that much more difficult.

That means the Scots could be drawn in a group with the likes of Serbia, Turkey, Czech Republic, Switzerland, or Austria as their pot 2 opponent.

For example, Scotland could be in a group with Spain, Switzerland, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. Please, no.

The top 12 group winners and the eight best runners-up go straight through, with the rest of the runners-up going into a play-off with the best Nations League non-qualified group winners.

If Scotland make a hash of that, then do not fear...

Uefa is reserving two spots for the two best-ranked host nations who have not qualified after the completion of the qualifying group stage.

It's now feasible this may come into play.

Going on the assumption England - who have just turned over world champions Spain - will qualify, that leaves Scotland, Wales and Ireland. Despite the qualifying draw being in Belfast, Northern Ireland aren't a host nation.

If one of them qualifies through other means, then happy days.

If they do not, then the Scots will need to hope they are not the lowest-ranked team among the three or they face being locked out of their own house party.

Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed thousands of drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines.

National Highways discovered issues with how speed cameras were activated last year , affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, has since detected further faults.

The Home Office has revoked the approval that allows the footage to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it would now end its contract with the company.

Roads minister Justin Madders told the BBC: "We can't take chances with this.

"If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have."

But he admitted that the system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year.

The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment.

The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14.

Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including patrols by National Highways traffic officers which have been stepped up.

In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways.

For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit.

The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year.

National Highways said the incidents represent fewer than two each day, compared with more than six million activations of speed cameras on the affected roads over the same period.

The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge plus the A1 approach junction to the A14.

National Highways has been contacted for comment.

Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle has said the government must act urgently to "level the playing field" for Royal Mail or risk the business becoming unviable.

He said he was concerned that the firm was being "undercut" by rival parcel delivery firms who did not employ staff under the same conditions.

Royal Mail, which is owned by International Distribution Services, has struggled in recent years with increased competition, fewer letters being sent and fines from the regulator for missing delivery targets.

A government spokesperson said it would consider whether further reforms are required to the parcel market after the watchdog, Ofcom, publishes its annual monitoring report in December.

Kyle had started to prepare officials at the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) to look at the delivery market for parcels shortly before he was replaced in his job by Jonathan Reynolds as business secretary in July.

He said a "crunch point" had been reached where the government had to make a decision about whether it wants Royal Mail "to be a viable proposition in the future".

He said his review would have looked at where the costs in that market lay and where the profit was being made, to see successful companies upheld "the values of business in Britain today".

"If we leave it another few years then Royal Mail will just become unviable and it will just collapse under the weight of having full-time employees," he said.

According to Royal Mail, 98% of its 130,000 workers are permanent employees, with rights to benefits including pensions, sick pay and holiday pay.

Some other parcel delivery companies use self-employed delivery drivers, with some offering an opt-in service that gives couriers limited additional benefits.

Royal Mail is also legally obliged to offer customers a "one price goes anywhere" service across the UK and to deliver first class letters six days a week to every address.

Kyle's proposed review would not have considered further changes to Royal Mail's universal service obligations or to terms and conditions for its staff.

Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle had planned to launch a review of the parcel delivery market

Royal Mail's performance has improved in recent months but it is still missing its targets for delivering first and second class post.

The firm was fined £21m in October 2025 for missing delivery targets in 2024/25.

Ofcom agreed last year to scrap second class deliveries on Saturdays and to reduce the target for delivering first class post within a day of collection to 90%.

A government spokesperson said the current business secretary had met Royal Mail and the Communication Workers Union, which represents postal workers, last week "to seek timely progress on improving their quality of service and to reiterate our commitment to the company's success."

DBT has also launched a consultation on tackling , external what it calls "bogus" self-employment, which it describes as "a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations".

Royal Mail has welcomed the consultation, and a spokesperson for the company claimed some parts of the delivery industry were "driving a race to the bottom" on employment standards and said it would "continue to push for a level playing field, with strong and enforceable standards across the industry."

Royal Mail misses delivery targets again but hails 'encouraging' signs

Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans

Many MPs across the UK have reported receiving high volumes of complaints from constituents about missed and delayed deliveries.

Shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said that Royal Mail's management needed to address the business's failings.

"Customers are being asked time and time again to pay increased prices, yet the service they're receiving is not improving," he said.

"Be in no doubt, this is not the fault of the hardworking postmen and women, it's the fault of Royal Mail's management.

"Nationalisation isn't the solution to this problem. Instead, we need ministers and Ofcom to bear down on Royal Mail's management to ensure they deliver on the improvements they've promised their customers."

The Communication Workers Union, which represents Royal Mail workers, is also putting pressure on ministers, with General Secretary Dave Ward calling for a "new model of ownership".

A trader in Nyamata market, Bugesera District, offered to mix a skin-lightening cream that could change a customer’s complexion within a week.

She quoted Rwf15,000 ($11), warned that the mixture could damage the hands and feet, and proceeded to prepare it after the reporter negotiated the price down to Rwf13,500 ($9).

The transaction exposes a market that has survived Rwanda’s ban on skin-bleaching products by changing its names, packaging and sales methods.

This story was adapted from an investigation by KigaliToday.com , the Kinyarwanda platform of Kigali Today Ltd and a partner to KT Press .

The investigation began after the reporter noticed people whose skin colour had changed dramatically. Some openly said they were using creams advertised on social media as solutions for dark spots, pimples and uneven skin tone.

A trader contacted by the investigating reporter said customers used different products, including creams containing hydroquinone and those marketed as Eclaircissant . She refused to discuss the ingredients over the phone, asking the reporter to visit his shop instead.

In the video footage below, our reporter discreetly films as the trader mixes the different products that they promise will offer best quality skin. The problem, though, the same mix has cause irreparable damage to other women.

The investigation also uncovered the experience of a woman who said skin-lightening mixtures had left her with dark, hardened fingers, discoloured feet and white patches between her fingers and toes.

She had started using the products after giving birth in 2020, hoping to restore her complexion. Over six years, she tried mixtures from five different traders, but says the damage has not fully healed.

In the YouTube video below, a victim of deadly bleaching cremes tells her horifying ordeal.

One trader blamed another for the skin problems and promised a better product. Another mixture also caused discolouration. She later bought creams imported from Burundi, but her skin developed several different shades, even though two other women who bought the same products reported no problems.

When the reporter visited the trader, she displayed products labelled Whitening , Brightening , Skin Lightening , Clear Skin and Eclaircissant .

She said a mixture containing hydroquinone could produce results within a week, but warned of possible problems on the hands and feet.

She mixed creams, boosters, vitamins, glycerine and a product he called Diproson , which he said prevented allergic reactions. The reporter paid Rwf13,500 and was instructed to apply the mixture twice daily.

Rwanda banned skin-bleaching products in 2013 and launched a campaign against their sale and use in 2018. But the trade continues.

In May 2025, police seized 689 bottles representing 31 varieties of skin-damaging products from three people in Kigali. The products had reportedly been brought from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Rubavu.

The Rwanda Food and Drugs Authority has listed more than 130 prohibited creams and related products. Some contain hydroquinone, steroids or mercury, substances associated with damage to the skin and other health risks.

Police say traders now use labels such as Brightening , Glowing and Clear Skin to disguise products, while some mixtures are prepared secretly in homes and beauty salons or sold through WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook and TikTok.

Dermatologist Dr Alice Amani Uwajeni says the products remain available despite the ban. She warns that changing their names does not make them safe.

He has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string of quirky arthouse films - so what clues can Robert Pattinson's past roles give us about what he might be like as James Bond?

Every actor creates a new James Bond, and Pattinson is one of the best in the business at crafting a memorable character.

The British actor can be an action man or an anti-hero, a romantic lead or a comic fool. He can be granite-faced or goofy, and everything in between.

"I was thinking about what the aspects of James Bond are, and he's done all of those throughout his career," says Paul Tweddle, host of the Heavy Spoilers film podcast , external .

He cites Pattinson's performance as a brooding heartthrob in teen vampire franchise Twilight, his suave and quick-witted secret agent in Christopher Nolan's Tenet, the withdrawn and focused title character in The Batman, and the ruthless and manipulative Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey.

Pattinson has "often been drawn to really dark fare", says Anna Smith, film critic and host of the Girls on Film podcast.

"Wouldn't it be interesting to see Bond go a little bit darker?" she suggested to the BBC's World Service. "But also what he's got, and I'd like him to do more of, is comedy. And goodness knows, we need a Bond who can handle humour."

Unusually for a James Bond actor, one word that has cropped up frequently is "weird".

Earlier this month, Pattinson was described as "the weirdest guy in Hollywood" by the Celebrating Cinema podcast , external .

"Pattinson is an actor who makes bold, interesting, risky choices. For such a handsome guy, he can bring the weird, and then some," wrote Chris Hewitt in Empire , external .

"About 0.07 seconds after the announcement, people were already anticipating the weird with his Bond. And they may well get their wish."

Pattinson (right) starred with Willem Dafoe in The Lighthouse in 2019

Variety's chief critic Guy Lodge said , external Pattinson's reputation as an actor "has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos", such as in more offbeat films like Good Time, The Lighthouse, Primetime and Mickey 17.

"Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play," Lodge added. "His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in The Odyssey is off on its own beam entirely."

Associated Press film critic Jake Coyle said , external smaller films like The Lighthouse and High Life show "Pattinson's proclivity for pushing boundaries".

"He's certainly the funniest and quickest to laugh James Bond we've had in decades," Coyle continued. "It will be interesting to see how much of his personality bleeds into Bond, or how much the tux stifles it."

Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond

Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007

So what do Pattinson's performances in some of his biggest films tell us about what to expect?

Pattinson in Tenet with Himesh Patel (left) and John David Washington (right)

Pattinson plays a dapper and enigmatic British agent in Christopher Nolan's time-bending 2020 thriller, as adept at bungeeing off an arms dealer's tower as he is delivering some deliciously dry wit.

"He's very suave, he's thinking on his feet," Tweddle says. "He's someone who's holding his cards close to his chest and not necessarily giving the game away.

"Tenet is the obvious one where Nolan's basically doing a kind of James Bond movie."

The Times' chief critic Kevin Maher agrees , external : "Pattinson has effectively played Bond already, when he effortlessly inhabited the role of the suave yet nonetheless lethal British spy Neil in Tenet.

"For many observers (including this one) that was the role. That was the audition. There was no turning back after Neil."

New York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson noted that Pattinson has picked up other "Bond-adjacent" roles. "The most obvious is Bruce Wayne, a.k.a. Batman, the wealthy playboy with a lair of tech toys and his own gussied-up automobile," she wrote , external .

"Wayne and Bond have a lot in common on paper, but in Pattinson's hands Wayne becomes emo, reclusive, awkward, with the hair of a '90s grunge rocker."

The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw also pointed out , external parallels with how Pattinson played "the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves's 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows - like Bond, used to working in secret".

Like Tenet, The Batman proved Pattinson is an expert at action scenes, whether that be jumping off a building or being involved in an explosive car chase with The Penguin.

"Batman is a really good example of where he's a withdrawn figure, someone who has his mind focused solely on a task, and I think that's a big part of what James Bond needs to be," Tweddle says.

However, Pattinson's 007 should be a little less brooding and aloof than his stony-faced Batman and Bruce Wayne.

Although Pattinson plays the villain in Nolan's Greek epic, Antinous's ruthlessness could come in handy when playing Bond, according to Tweddle.

"I think Robert Pattinson also has quite a psychotic side to him, which a lot of the James Bond books delve into - how he's a killer, and he needs to have that side to him," he says.

"What he's done in The Odyssey shows he can be manipulative, and connive and make certain plans, which is what a spy needs to do."

Collider's Collier Jennings named , external The Odyssey, along with Tenet and The Batman, as films that show Pattinson is "the perfect" fit for Bond.

"All three roles carry an element that makes James Bond work," Jennings wrote.

"Batman has the combat skills and subterfuge you'd need to be a spy of Bond's caliber, not to mention the cutting edge hardware.

"Neil has a great grasp on the intricacies of pulling off complex covert operations.

"Antonius walks with a swagger and arrogance that either makes you love him or hate him."

Pattinson's current film sees him play real-life NBC journalist Chris Hansen, who carried out sting operations on paedophiles for TV show To Catch a Predator.

It again demonstrates Pattinson's range as an actor and his ability to take on complex roles - he balances the portrayal of Hansen, not as a villain but equally not as a hero.

"He's very much face-to-face with the predators in the room, and he's controlling the situation," Tweddle explains.

"It's very confrontational and demands a certain amount of power. Being able to control the room like that is also quite transferable to James Bond, and interrogations are a big part of what he does."

Pattinson will next be seen playing shape-shifting villain Scytale in the forthcoming third instalment of the epic sci-fi series - directed by Denis Villeneuve.

The pair's reunion for the next Bond movie is not a coincidence. Villeneuve's experience of working with Pattinson on the film may have been the deciding factor when casting James Bond.

"The thing I adore with Robert Pattinson is that when you roll cameras, there's always a certain moment where you have no idea what will happen. He is an explosion in front of the camera," the director told Time , external .

"He has an incredible imagination and is a very playful actor, and a very creative actor, always trying to bring new ways of expressing himself and always trying to surprise me."

Surprising, bold, weird? One thing is for certain, Pattinson's James Bond is going to be interesting.

Perezida Paul Kagame mu ijwi rye bwite, yivugiye uburyo mu myaka isaga umunani ishize, Ubufaransa bwamwegereye bukamubwira buti "nyakubahwa twifuzaga ko muduha Louise Mushikiwabo, akiyamamaza ku mwanya w'umunyamabanga mukuru wa OIF, kuko tubona aramutse agiriwe icyizere yatanga umusanzu mwiza."

Perezida Kagame yabanje kwibaza impamvu yatanga umukozi we mwiza, wari Minisitiri w'Ububanyi n'Amahanga icyo gihe, wenda akaba yanatsindwa kuko ari amatora, kandi nyamara yari afite aho atanga umusanzu mu rwamubyaye, ariko bigeze aho, ati "reka mbaze nyirubwite numve niba na we ubwe abishaka.'

Umukuru w'Igihugu iyi nkuru yayibwiye Louise Mushikiwabo, na we aravuga ati "Sinzi impamvu yabyo, nta n'ubwo mbona inyungu yabyo."

Igihe cyo kwiyamamaza cyasanze u Rwanda rwaramaze kubyakira, no kwemeza Louise Mushikiwabo ko yajya guhatana n'abandi agatanga umusanzu, mu gihe yaramuka atowe.

Mushikiwabo yariyamamaje, aratorwa, ndetse ageze mu kazi ahindura umuryango, arawagura, awuha imicungire myiza n'umwuka mwiza, ubuzima buragaruka.

Ni yo mpamvu, mu gihe cyo gutora muri manda ya kabiri, Mushikiwabo yahise yongera ariyamamaza, maze aratsinda.

Muri Manda ya gatatu, Igihugu gisanzwe kizamura ijwi iyo u Rwanda rubonye icyiza, ari cyo Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo, cyarashakuje, maze gishyiramo umukandida wacyo, abantu bagira ngo biciriye aho.

Tshisekedi ati mureke tubimene mpombe n'u Rwanda ruhombe

Mushikiwabo yakoze urugendo rwo kwiyamamaza, nk'uko na bagenzi be batatu bandi babikoze, barimo n'uwa Congo.

Umukandida watanzwe na Congo, mbere na mbere yaje atwibutsa ko uwo mwanya nta wundi ukwiye uretse we, kuko ari umukobwa w'intwari Lumumba.

Mu gihe inama yari hafi kuba, Perezida wa DRC Felix Tshisekedi yaratangiye aravuga ati "Muzi n'ibindi? Umukandida w'u Rwanda aramutse atowe, twebwe Congo turahita tuva muri Francophonie."

Akibivuga ibikuba byaracitse, maze Perezida w'Ubufaransa, Emmanuel Macron atangira gusaba u Rwanda ati "Mwo kabyara mwe, mwatwemereye mugakuramo Louise Mushikiwabo, tukareba ko umunyamuryango yakwishima?"

Ubwoba Macron yari afite, ni uko ngo DRC ari yo ifite umubare munini w'abavuga Igifaransa ugereranyije n'ibindi bihugu, ku buryo yibwiraga ati "Congo iramutse igiye, umuryango waba usenyutse."

U Rwanda, igihugu kigendera ku mategeko, ntabwo kijya gikoresha amarangamutima muri diplomasi, n'ahandi hose. Rwarabyanze, rubibutsa ko ayo ari amategeko umuryango washyizeho.

Aha ni ho Tshisekedi yabonye ko nta mikino, araviga ati "reka nkuremo umukandida wanjye, wenda na bo barahita bakuramo uwabo, kuko wenda baranga ko umunyekongo yayobora.'

Aha na ho, u Rwanda rwerekanye ko kubahiriza amategeko ari byo rureba, ibindi ntacyo bivuze.

Ikibazo cyarakomeye, abarakara bararakara, abasohoka mu nama baragenda, u Rwanda rukabareba rukababwira ruti 'sawa rero'.

Mu bwumvikane bw'Abakuru b'Ibihugu bwagezweho bigoranye, bageze aho bemeza ko Louise Mushikiwabo ayobora umwaka twakwita nk'aho ari inzibacyuho, hanyuma agahindura amategeko atuma umuryango uhura n'ibyuho bituma udashobora gutera intambwe igana imbere, ndetse agategura n'amatora y'uzamusimbura.

Muri ibi byose, umu chou wacu nta cyaha wamushinja

Louise Mushikiwabo, abenshi mu Rwanda bakunze kwita Umu chou, cyangwa Mushiki w'aba Chou, si umu Gen-z cyangwa umuntu muto, haba mu myaka, haba muri Politiki na dipolomasi n'ubuyobozi muri rusange.

Ahubwo, aka kabyiniriro, katurutse ku rukundo akunda igihugu cye, ku buryo n'iyo abwira abanyarwanda, ababwira nk'inshuti ze, abantu bo mu rugo.

Hari n'aho ababwira ati 'aba chou, ndabakumbuye trop", maze ubutumwa bwe bukanyura mu kirere cya Paris, bugahinguranya inyanja bukadusanga i Kigali. Ubwo rero umuntu ubabaje Mushikiwabo, aba ababaje abantu benshi bamukunda.

Nuko rero...nk'umuyobozi, Mushikiwabo yari yateguye amatora ya OIF muri rusange mu mucyo, maze no ku giti cye, yiyamamaza neza ntawe ahutaje, yuzuza ibisabwa abakandida bose.

Icyaha rukumbi Congo ishobora kuba imushinga, ni uko yabaye umuyobozi wa OIF werekanye itandukaniro, agahuza abanyamuryango, akabaha imishinga ikomeye, harimo n'iyagiye muri Congo ubwayo.

Icyabababaje nuko umukandida w'Umunyarwanda yakomeje gukundwa, kandi bashaka ko yangwa, bakumva u Rwanda rukomeza kuvugwa, kandi bo bashaka kuvuga ngo "mubambe! U Rwanda murubambe, kwisha maneno"!

Muri iki cyumweru dushoje, umu chou w'Abanyarwanda Congo n'abambari bayo barimo u Burundi baramubabaje, bamutwerera ibibazo adafite cyangwa atateje, ahubwo bo ubwabo bananiwe gukemura kubera ubwikunde, ivanguramoko n'ubusambo.

Bafashe kandidatire ye barayigaragura, barayihindukiza, bayikoza hirya no hino, atari uko hari ibiburamo, ahubwo ubwenge bwe n'umusanzu yahaye OIF warabariye bishima mu mutwe.

Mwibaze kuba wateguye inama, ukakira abanyacyubahiro ku buryo butangaje, ariko aho kugira ngo bazane amagambo y'ishimwe, umwe agahaguruka ati 'ntitugushaka, n'iyo wagira ute'.

Icyiza gusa, ni uko byakorwaga n'abantu basanzwe bazwi ho kubura umuco karande, kuko abandi banyamuryango bashimye.

Uyu munsi, Abanyekongo baragira bati "twatsinze, icyo twashakaga nuko adahabwa manda ya gatatu," nuko bakongeraho n'andi magambo atari meza, buri wese bitewe n'uburere buciriritse afite.

Mushikiwabo yoherejwe muri misiyo n'u Rwanda, kandi ubutumwa yabushohoje neza. Igihe cye nikirangira, u Rwanda ruzamukoresha ku bundi buryo bwabigennye. Nk'umuntu wayoboye neza, agomba kubahwa n'abanyamuryango bose, akazibukirwa ibyiza byose yandikishije muri uriya muryango, maze ibya Congo bakareka Congo igakomeza kubyigaraguramo nk'uko bisanzwe.

Ahasigaye, nk'uko akunda kubivuga, "ibisigaye ni problemes gerables".

Few would have predicted that Carlo Ancelotti would be facing the wrath of a Brazil legend just 18 months into his tenure as head coach of the Brazil national team.

But Romario, Brazil's fourth-highest scorer behind only Neymar, Pele and Ronaldo, has publicly demanded that legendary manager Ancelotti be relieved of his duties not once but twice in the last week alone.

It all started after Brazil suffered a 3-2 friendly defeat by Japan on Friday thanks to a controversial stoppage-time winner from Tatsuhiro Sakamoto.

Ancelotti received a red card for dissent in the aftermath - the first of his international management career, as Barcelona forward Raphinha also saw red.

And in the wake of that defeat, despite it being a friendly, Romario quickly took to social media to air his frustrations about the former Real Madrid boss.

"Ancelotti, enough is enough! Pack your bags and leave!" he wrote on Instagram.

"Nobody questions your history. You are one of the greatest coaches world football has ever seen, but that was at club level."

Brazil were eliminated by Norway in the round of 16 at the 2026 World Cup, a result which ensured they failed to qualify for the quarter-finals for the first time since 1990.

And Romario alluded to this too, stating that the country "can't take the risk of throwing another World Cup in the trash - the time to act is now!"

The Brazil boss has been in the game long enough to know how to deal with all sorts of opinions.

He has won the Champions League a record five times as a head coach and won the league title in all of Europe's top five divisions, along with multiple domestic cups.

But his record with Brazil is far from perfect. Across 21 matches, they have recorded 12 wins, four draws and five defeats.

However, while Ancelotti acknowledges the need for improvement, he emphasised the fact that it is still "a new project."

Speaking before Brazil's friendly with Singapore on Tuesday the Italian said: "In a democratic country with freedom of speech, everyone is allowed to express their opinion.

"It's not up to me to say whether the things he says are correct, wrong or just stupid. The truth is that Romario talks a lot. A lot. It's his right."

Despite the criticism he has faced, Ancelotti feels Brazil are on the right track and who is to tell him otherwise when you look at his track record?

"I really like what we're doing," he said.

You would have thought that would have been enough to let it lie for the time being.

But before Brazil had even kicked a ball in their next friendly against Singapore, Romario was speaking out again.

The former striker, who is the ninth-highest goalscorer in football history with 784 goals, doubled down on his calls for Ancelotti to be sacked.

"I talk a lot because when it comes to the national team, I have size, weight and power of speech," Romario, 60, said.

"I do not speak to gain followers, I do not speak for people to like me. I speak my mind.

"I have worn this shirt for many years and I am pretty sure I was one of the ones that helped the little yellow be respected all over the world."

He said he respected Ancelotti but added he hadn't "added anything new" to the national side.

"We will find another coach who will do a better job than you. And I'm saying this to your face, not through a message, including to the president of the CBF, who is long overdue to fire you."

Brazil faced Singapore in their final match of 2026 on Tuesday and won 7-0 .

Real Madrid forward Vinicius Junior, who has come under scrutiny of his own so far this season, scored a hat-trick within the opening 21 minutes while Bournemouth winger Rayan and Chelsea's Estevao were also on the scoresheet.

It's a result that may bring a pause to proceedings in this war of words for now. However, if this last seven days has proved anything, it's that this saga is likely far from over.

The police chiefs of Rwanda and Uganda have signed an implementation framework aimed at strengthening cooperation between the two countries’ law enforcement institutions.

The agreement was signed on Tuesday, November 17, during a bilateral meeting between Rwanda’s Inspector General of Police, CG Felix Namuhoranye, and his Ugandan counterpart, IGP Abbas Byakagaba, at the Rwanda National Police (RNP) General Headquarters in Kacyiru, Kigali.

Namuhoranye received Byakagaba and his delegation for discussions focused on strengthening the existing relationship between the two police institutions and enhancing cooperation for the mutual benefit of both countries.

The framework will guide the implementation of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed by the two institutions last year.

The meeting is part of efforts by the Rwanda National Police and Uganda Police Force to deepen their institutional ties and cooperation in areas of mutual interest.

Arsenal are in advanced talks with defender Piero Hincapie over a new contract.

Hincapie, 24, joined the Gunners last summer from Bayer Leverkusen, initially on loan, with the Gunners activating an option to make the move permanent at the end of the season.

The Ecuador international has established himself as a key member of Mikel Arteta's squad, making 47 appearances in all competitions.

The versatile defender's existing deal still has over four years left to run - but he is now set to sign a 12-month extension on improved terms.

Elsewhere, the club intend to open talks with left-back Riccardo Calafiori, 24, over renewing his deal.

The Italy international has become a crucial part of Arteta's plans since his arrival from Bologna in 2024.

His current deal expires in the summer of 2029, but it is expected talks over an extension will begin in the not too distant future.

Arsenal are on a contract renewal drive, with the club set to confirm new deals for Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and goalkeeper David Raya.

A funeral was held for Fadwa al-Fahidat in the village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Tuesday

A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.

There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.

According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response.

There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.

They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.

All settlements are illegal under international law.

Medics say Palestinians and Israelis were wounded in the incident on Monday evening

Palestinian reports said Fadwa al-Fahidat, who was 72, was shot outside her home on Monday evening and that, hearing the news, her son sped to the scene in his car.

He then collided with an empty Israeli vehicle parked outside his family home and settlers standing nearby were injured, they said. The settlers then began shooting, the reports said.

The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".

Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat." It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.

The IDF said that Israeli security forces were sent to the scene and were pursuing suspects.

Doctors at a hospital in Jericho said that al-Fahidat was shot in the head. Several other Palestinians and Israelis were injured, reports said.

The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.

Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.

A group of settlers set up a new outpost in al-Duyuk al-Tahta earlier this month (file photo)

In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.

The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.

Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.

It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".

The UK government said on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary David Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.

A man has been convicted of a hate crime after directing racist insults at Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe during a La Liga match at Real Oviedo in 2025.

A court in Asturias, the northern Spanish region where Oviedo is based, handed down a guilty verdict against the man for the abuse at the Carlos Tartiere Stadium.

The defendant was sentenced to 11 months in prison, alongside a fine and a number of additional disqualifications.

The prison sentence has been suspended on the condition that he does not enter any stadium hosting official sporting competitions for a period of two years.

The ruling represents another legal development in Spanish football's ongoing battle against racism, with Real Madrid continuing to pursue criminal action against individuals responsible for discriminatory abuse directed at the club's players.

The club highlighted the latest conviction follows previous successful legal cases involving racist insults aimed at Vinicius Jr at Valencia's Mestalla , Mallorca's Son Moix, Rayo Vallecano's Vallecas and Real Valladolid's Jose Zorrilla stadiums.

Real Madrid acted as a private prosecutor in the Asturias case and says the club will continue to take legal action in other incidents involving racist behaviour.

"Real Madrid reaffirms its commitment to combating racism and eradicating any racist behavior in football and sports," a club statement said.

It comes after Spain's head coach Luis de la Fuente insisted there was no racism in Spain or in Spanish football before their Nations League meeting with England in Madrid on Sunday.

De la Fuente was asked whether the fact Thomas Tuchel had said he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the match showed that more work needed to be done to tackle racism in Spanish football.

But he responded: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

The Spanish Football Federation was fined last month and ordered to partially close a stadium after supporters directed Islamophobic and xenophobic chants towards Muslims during a match against Egypt in Barcelona.

Passengers arriving at Kigali International Airport (Photo by The New Times)

Rwanda earned US$604 million from international visitors in 2025, contributing to a regional travel economy that generated nearly US$12 billion, according to a new report by the East African Community (EAC) Secretariat.

The survey, Travel Is the Leading Contributor to EAC Service Export Earnings , places Rwanda fifth among EAC Partner States in travel service export earnings, behind Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda and Somalia.

Travel service export earnings represent money spent by people visiting a country from abroad, including expenditure on accommodation, food, transport and other services.

Unlike broader tourism revenue, which can also include spending by domestic tourists, travel service export earnings specifically capture spending by non-residents. They also cover people travelling for business and other purposes, not just those on holiday.

Across the EAC, total travel earnings reached US$11.991 billion in 2025, making travel the largest contributor to the region’s service export earnings.

Rwanda accounted for approximately 5% of this total, with its US$604 million earnings putting it ahead of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Burundi and South Sudan.

Tanzania and Kenya dominated the regional market, generating US$4.411 billion and US$3.826 billion, respectively. Their combined earnings of US$8.237 billion represented approximately 69% of the EAC total.

The two countries also recorded the highest numbers of foreign visitors in the region. Kenya received approximately 2.6 million foreign visitors in 2025, while Tanzania welcomed about 2.3 million.

Uganda ranked third with US$1.778 billion in travel earnings, followed by Somalia with US$1.228 billion. Rwanda’s US$604 million placed it fifth.

At the lower end of the regional rankings, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) recorded US$140 million in travel service export earnings, while Burundi earned US$3 million and South Sudan US$1 million.

Rwanda’s US$604 million earnings were more than four times those of the DRC and significantly higher than the figures recorded by Burundi and South Sudan.

The data highlights the growing importance of travel services to the EAC economy. Their contribution to regional service export earnings increased from 31% in 2020 to 55% in 2025, overtaking transportation, which accounted for 25%, while all other services combined contributed 20%.

Overall, EAC service export earnings increased from US$12.2 billion in 2021 to US$21.6 billion in 2025, representing a 77% rise over the period.

The figures underline the importance of international visitors to the region’s economies, with their spending generating foreign exchange and supporting economic activity and employment across the EAC.

A funding boost for the NHS has been included in Plaid Cymru's first budget, but other public services could still feel the pinch.

Despite an extra £500m to cut waiting lists, spending on health will not rise as quickly as it has in recent years.

Money has also been set aside to negotiate a crucial political deal on the budget – the first since Plaid won power at May's Senedd election.

With no overall majority in the Senedd, the party's Welsh government needs support from political opponents to approve its tax and spending plans.

Wales to make £100 energy payments but Plaid ministers say Budget leaves them with cuts

Announcing the budget, Finance Minister Elin Jones said the "public finances are tight" with the funding available to run day-to-day services expected to shrink 0.5% next year.

An extra £500m for health represents an increase of 2.1% after allowing for inflation - the rate at which costs are rising.

But this is well below the historical average rise of 3.6%.

Funding for local councils will increase by £176m, but some councils could see their funding rise by as little as 0.4% in real terms.

Council leaders have warned about a funding shortfall because of growing demand and inflation.

There is no change to the rate of income tax that the Welsh government controls, nor to the land transaction tax that is paid by people buying properties.

Jones said the budget "concentrates resources where they will make the biggest difference to people's lives and we will make every pound count".

She said: "This budget is a break with the past.

"It is a reset in how Wales spends public money, and it lays the foundations for everything this government wants to achieve over this Senedd term, including a stronger NHS, support for local councils and more help with childcare."

Winning the budget vote, due to happen next February, will be the biggest test Plaid has faced since forming a government.
