The Africa Midwifery Acceleration Forum is underway in Kigali.

KIGALI – Africa needs an estimated 435,000 additional midwives across Eastern and Southern Africa, North Africa and the Arab region to strengthen maternal and newborn healthcare, as the continent confronts a shortage of skilled professionals capable of preventing millions of deaths.

The scale of the deficit comes against evidence that expanding access to midwife-delivered healthcare could prevent 67% of maternal deaths, 64% of newborn deaths and 65% of stillbirths by 2035, potentially saving 4.3 million lives every year.

When properly educated, regulated and supported, midwives can deliver approximately 90% of essential sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn and adolescent health interventions, making them central to preventing deaths and improving access to healthcare.

Lydia Zigomo, UNFPA Regional Director for East and Southern Africa, presented the figures at the Africa Midwifery Acceleration Forum, which is underway in Kigali, bringing together over 200 policymakers, health professionals, midwifery leaders and development partners from across the continent.

She said Eastern and Southern Africa alone faces an estimated shortage of 307,000 midwives, while North Africa and the Arab region need another 128,000.

Lydia Zigomo, UNFPA Regional Director for East and Southern Africa.

“Investment in midwifery is among the most effective ways to improve health outcomes while strengthening economies. Even a 25% increase in coverage every five years could save 2.2 million lives annually,” Zigomo said.

The figures expose a major gap between what African health systems could achieve and their current capacity to provide essential care, particularly in rural communities, fragile settings and areas where women struggle to access qualified professionals.

Jean Kaseya, Director-General of the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), said approximately 179,000 African women died from pregnancy-related causes in 2023, representing nearly 70% of the estimated 260,000 maternal deaths recorded worldwide that year.

“What makes this tragedy particularly unacceptable is that most of these deaths are preventable. We have the scientific knowledge, we know the interventions that work, yet we continue to lose mothers and newborns because our health systems are not delivering what they should,” Kaseya said in a recorded address.

He challenged governments to look beyond the number of professionals trained and examine whether they are employed, deployed where they are needed and equipped to provide quality care.

“How can government invest in training health professionals and then fail to create positions for them to serve our people? How can we continue discussing maternal mortality while qualified professionals remain at home unable to practice?” he asked.

“A trained midwife without employment cannot save a mother. And an employed midwife without essential supplies cannot deliver the quality of care that every woman deserves,” he noted.

Dr Yvan Butera, Minister of State for Health addressing delegates.

Rwanda, which is hosting the continental gathering, offers an example of how expanding midwifery education and access to skilled birth attendance can change maternal health outcomes, although challenges remain.

Dr Yvan Butera, Minister of State for Health, said the proportion of women giving birth in health facilities with assistance from skilled health professionals has risen to 98%, compared with just one in four women receiving skilled assistance at birth approximately 25 years ago.

“Just three years ago, every year, we were training around 72 midwives. This year, we enrolled 1,050 midwives that are starting training,” Butera said.

The expansion is part of Rwanda’s broader 4×4 Health Workforce Strategy, which seeks to quadruple the country’s health workforce. The first graduates under the programme were expected to enter health facilities soon.

Butera said neonatal deaths account for nearly half of all deaths among children under five in Rwanda, meaning one in every two children who die before their fifth birthday does not survive beyond the first 28 days.

“The midwife is usually the first guardian of that child in the first hour, the first day, the first week. It is therefore important to invest in professionals who attend mothers and newborns during the most vulnerable stages of life,” he said.

Dr Olive Bazirete, Dean of the University of Rwanda’s School of Nursing and Midwifery.

Rwanda’s maternal mortality ratio has also fallen from more than 1,000 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2000 to 149 today, according to Dr Olive Bazirete, Dean of the University of Rwanda’s School of Nursing and Midwifery.

The country has expanded its midwifery training capacity from one institution to 11, reflecting efforts to strengthen the profession through higher education and investment in the health workforce.

International partnerships have also contributed to the expansion of midwifery education in Rwanda. An India-UN Development Partnership Fund project has supported the training of 488 students over the past two years, including 338 who received scholarships in 2026.

Beyond the health benefits, the economic returns from investing in midwifery are evident. In Zambia, an investment estimated at US$241 million to achieve 95% universal coverage of midwife-delivered healthcare could generate US$2.3 billion in economic benefits.

The three-day Kigali forum is expected to validate the Continental Midwifery Acceleration Roadmap for Africa 2026–2035, providing a framework for countries to strengthen midwifery education, regulation, leadership, financing and deployment.

The success of that ambition will depend on whether governments translate commitments into employment opportunities, adequate budgets and better working conditions.

“To our midwives today, I want to express my profound respect. You deserve more than appreciation and recognition. You deserve employment, investment, decent working conditions, and a meaningful voice in shaping our health systems,” Kaseya said.

Lieke van de Wiel, UNICEF Country Representative to Rwanda spoke on behalf of the UN Resident Coordinator.

MN202611_dbv0eanwv4.t:
Channel 4's chief executive has admitted she doesn't know how many complaints of sexual misconduct were received about Married at First Sight UK, despite a six-month external review into the hit TV show.

When asked by MPs, Priya Dogra said: "I'm not sure I have the details," adding that the review looked specifically at the claims of three women featured in a BBC Panorama.

Married at First Sight UK was cancelled after Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members , while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations.

Separately, Dogra said the broadcaster "cannot apologise enough" to a former employee who twice made complaints about Russell Brand and felt they weren't properly handled.

Dogra said it was "almost unforgivable" that the woman said she complained to Channel 4 in 2009 and again in 2023.

Brand is serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after recently being found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegations

Married at First Sight UK, known as MAFS UK, had been running for 10 seasons and was one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.

The Panorama investigation in May heard from three women who made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny:

One woman said her on-screen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.

A second woman told both Channel 4 and production company CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her on-screen husband. Her episodes were still aired.

A third woman accused her on-screen husband of sexual misconduct.

All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.

A review was commissioned into MAFS UK by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster with details of the allegations.

Earlier this month, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

Speaking to MPs on the House of Commons culture and media committee on Tuesday, Dogra was repeatedly asked if she knew how many allegations Channel 4 and CPL had received over the years that MAFS UK was on air.

"I looked specifically into those instances [the three women], I did not do a broad sweep of every episode or every season of the show. That is not what the terms of reference for the show were," she responded.

"If there are others, we would take them seriously and look into them on the same basis."

Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.

"You're saying your inquiry didn't actually look at how many complaints were made into this show in total?" replied the committee's chair, Dame Caroline Dinenage.

"The inquiry looked at our handling of these specific incidents," responded Dogra.

When pushed about who would know how many allegations of harm had been received over the years, Dogra said that information would be held internally between Channel 4 and CPL.

Dogra, who started as Channel 4 chief executive earlier this year, also said she was "frankly uncomfortable" with some of the changes proposed by the review into MAFS UK - such as 24-hour CCTV and lockable bedrooms - hence her reason for axing the show.

Channel 4's bosses were also questioned at length about Brand by MPs in the hearing.

Brand's work on Channel 4 included hosting Big Brother sister show Big Brother's Big Mouth and its celebrity equivalent from 2004 to 2007, a chat show in 2006, and appearing on Big Fat Quiz of the Year.

Addressing Dogra and Channel 4's chairman Geoff Cooper, MPs said the member of staff who made two complaints about Brand "fell through the cracks".

In response, Dogra said: "I'm not sure we can apologise enough as an organisation for putting her through that twice. We have apologised in public in the past and in private."

She accepted that the woman's complaints were "not handled properly" and added that "it's almost unforgivable that happened twice".

When asked by the committee if junior members of staff could raise complaints against a star without fear of losing their job, Dogra replied she "can't say 100%" that that would be the case.

Woman who accuses Russell Brand of rape says prison message 'upsetting'

"What I can do is set the standard, set the tone, make sure that the facilities are available, make sure that my staff and the production companies understand the repercussions of not complying, and understand the kind of culture that I'm trying to set, and we're trying to set as an industry."

She also said she found the "cultural personality" around Brand "horrendous".

"I find it distasteful, and I look at the jokes... that is the lowest form of humour, because these are jokes that are made at the expense of someone else's physical safety.

"I don't believe it should have been acceptable then, and I certainly don't think it's acceptable now."

During the session, Dame Caroline also put to Channel 4 bosses that in both the MAFS UK and Brand cases, the broadcaster appeared like "a child with their hand in the cookie jar".

The committee chairwoman asked: "To what extent can you reassure us that Channel 4's priority is genuinely the welfare of the staff who work there, the staff who have worked there, and the people who take part in your shows - rather than purely when the world is looking at you and you suddenly feel that you've got a reputational reason to take a look at these shows?"

Dogra responded by saying that when Channel 4 commissioned the review, "we didn't even know whether the Panorama programme would be made".

She added: "We had received a right-to-reply letter and the programme came out six weeks later, but it equally it could not have been made. We always intended to do the review."

In the instance of the woman who tried to complain about Brand, she added: "I'm not sure there are more apologies we can give. Because none of those things should've happened."

England batter Jacob Bethell left the tour of Australia at the weekend

Jacob Bethell will miss England's Test tour of South Africa because he requires more surgery on the knee injury that has kept him out since July.

Batter Bethell was due to make his return in the ongoing white-ball tour of Australia, but had to leave that trip at the weekend after suffering what England described as a "setback" in training.

The 23-year-old has met with a specialist and, as first reported by the Telegraph, will have a second operation on his right knee. There is no timeframe on when he could return to play.

England are yet to confirm Bethell's replacement for the three Tests against the Proteas. They will choose from the England Lions, who arrive in South Africa before the Test squad.

When the Warwickshire man missed the three Tests against Pakistan during the home summer, his place in the England squad went to Ollie Pope.

Bethell has not played since the third one-day international against India at Lord's in July, when he suffered discomfort in his knee.

In his absence from the Test side during the Pakistan series, Emilio Gay opened and Jordan Cox took Bethell's slot at number three.

It was expected that one of Gay or Cox would have to drop out of the starting XI in South Africa to make way for Bethell's return.

When England announced their touring squad last week, selector Marcus North said that no decisions had been made on the make-up of the first-choice top six.

Now, in Bethell's continued absence, Gay and Cox will have further opportunities to make claims for a long-term place in the Test side.

Surrey's Pope has not played for England since the third Ashes Test against Australia in Adelaide in December of last year.

He was due to be with the Lions in South Africa on a tour that overlaps with the Test series and appears the most likely candidate to replace Bethell.

If England opt against Pope, Somerset's James Rew and uncapped Durham opener Ben McKinney have both been in strong form on the Lions' recent white-ball tour of the West Indies.

This latest setback is a significant blow to Bethell, who looked to have cemented his place in the Test side with a sparkling century in the final Ashes Test in Sydney in January.

But the knee injury cut short his summer, meaning he missed The Hundred, the Pakistan series, white-ball matches against Sri Lanka, then the limited-overs tours of Pakistan and Australia.

The second surgery would also leave him as a doubt for England's other winter Tests: two in Bangladesh in February and the one-off 150th anniversary day-nighter against Australia in Melbourne in March.

Bethell's absence from the South Africa tour was confirmed on the day he was released by Indian Premier League champions Royal Challengers Bengaluru.

The left-hander spent two seasons with RCB, making nine appearances. His limited opportunities with the two-time winners have led to regular questions as to whether his time would be better spent playing in the County Championship.

England are already without Josh Tongue for the first Test against South Africa in Johannesburg, beginning on 17 December. The pace bowler will be at home for the birth of his second child.

North has previously confirmed that England will call on fast-bowling reserves from the Lions to cover for Tongue.

A team of Scientists From 20 Countries are in the United Arab Emirates converging their skills to experiment the possiblity of effectively growing tomatoes in desert conditions.

Details indicate that the Scientists are stress-testing technologies to grow tomatoes, cucumbers, melons, and berries in an environment where temperatures top 50°C (122°F) and groundwater is salty.

In the deserts of the United Arab Emirates, rain comes about once a year, and when it does, it floods.

The sun is relentless, with temperatures regularly topping 50C (122F). The groundwater is salty. The soil, if you can call it that, is sand.

The scientists are converged at a U$200 million farming-tech incubator in the UAE actively testing how to make desert farming commercially viable.

Rwanda’s economic outlook has received renewed confidence from international financial markets after global credit-rating agency Standard & Poor’s (S&P Global Ratings) maintained the country’s B+ sovereign credit rating, citing strong economic growth, improved public financial management and a favourable structure of external debt.

The latest assessment reflects the country’s continued ability to sustain economic expansion while managing public spending and securing long-term financing for major development projects.

S&P noted that the economy grew by 9.3% in 2025 before recording approximately 10% year-on-year growth during the first half of 2026, driven largely by strong performance in manufacturing and services.

The agency projects economic growth of 7.5% in 2026, followed by an average of approximately 7% annually between 2027 and 2029.

The projections are supported by continued investment in infrastructure, expanding services, construction and manufacturing activities.

Sound management of public finances was another important factor supporting the rating. S&P projects that the fiscal deficit for the 2025/26 financial year will reach approximately 4.9% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), lower than the initially planned 5.7%.

The improvement is attributed to higher-than-expected tax revenues and reduced expenditure, partly resulting from more favourable financing arrangements for the New Kigali International Airport project.

The agency also highlighted the country’s debt composition, noting that more than 87% of external debt consists of concessional loans, which generally carry lower interest rates and longer repayment periods than commercial borrowing.

According to the Ministry of Finance’s September 2026 Public Debt Statistical Bulletin, total public and publicly guaranteed debt stood at Rwf17.85 trillion by June 2026, equivalent to 69.1% of GDP, down from 74.8% a year earlier.

The relatively high share of concessional financing helps limit immediate repayment pressures and gives the government greater flexibility to invest in long-term infrastructure and development programmes.

The New Kigali International Airport also features prominently in the economic outlook, with S&P recognising its potential to strengthen international connectivity, expand tourism, facilitate trade and position the country as a regional transport and business hub.

The project has benefited from an innovative financing arrangement involving the World Bank Group’s International Development Association (IDA) and Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA).

The arrangement helped reduce expenditure on the airport’s second phase by Rwf168.2 billion in 2026.

The airport is expected to begin full commercial operations around mid-2028, potentially providing additional momentum to the country’s aviation, tourism and logistics sectors.

External financial developments have also contributed to the positive assessment.

Remittances from citizens living abroad increased by 31.1% during the first half of 2026, while mineral exports recorded strong growth.

These developments helped narrow the country’s external deficit to 10.9% of GDP, compared with 13.4% during the corresponding period a year earlier.

S&P also projects that usable foreign currency reserves will average approximately $2.3 billion between 2026 and 2029, providing an important buffer against external economic shocks and supporting the country’s capacity to meet international payment obligations.

The agency further recognised progress under the International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme, noting that the government met all the targets assessed during the first review of its 38-month Extended Credit Facility arrangement. The first disbursement under the programme was released in October 2026.

The programme supports economic reforms, improved public financial management, domestic revenue mobilisation and long-term debt sustainability.

However, S&P cautioned that the economy remains exposed to external pressures, particularly rising international prices of fuel, food and fertilisers linked to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.

Such developments could increase inflation and put additional pressure on household spending and government expenditure.

The government has responded through targeted subsidies for diesel and fertilisers, while the National Bank of Rwanda has tightened credit conditions to contain inflation.

S&P expects inflation to ease to approximately 8% in 2027, although maintaining price stability will remain important for sustaining economic growth.

A B+ sovereign credit rating is classified as speculative grade, meaning that the country has the capacity to meet its financial obligations but remains vulnerable to adverse economic and financial conditions. Investment-grade ratings begin at BBB- on S&P’s scale.

Maintaining the B+ rating with a stable outlook therefore signals that the agency expects the country’s credit position to remain broadly steady under its current economic projections.

Sovereign credit ratings are important because they influence how international investors, commercial lenders and development finance institutions assess the risks associated with financing a country.

A stronger credit profile can improve access to international capital and potentially help reduce borrowing costs over time.

The latest assessment reinforces confidence in the country’s economic growth prospects, fiscal management and ability to attract long-term development financing, while highlighting the importance of continued reforms, responsible borrowing and economic diversification to sustain that progress.

Still Game is set for a return to the stage in 2028

Seven years ago, Scotland's most beloved pensioners climbed to the top of Ben Lomond and reached the big Clansman in the sky.

But now, Jack Jarvis and Victor McDade have been resurrected as Still Game returns to the stage for a special run of shows.

The stage show, Still Game Live: Heaven Sent, will have a 10-date run at the Ovo Hydro in Glasgow from February 2028.

Creators Ford Kiernan and Greg Hemphill joked they had a "fear of moving on" after announcing the characters' return.

The ninth and final series of the BBC comedy aired in 2019.

However, the last appearance of the duo came in another stage show, Still Game: The Final Farewell, later the same year.

Still Game duo say no more Jack and Victor

Jack and Victor return as Still Game becomes a comic book

Kiernan and Hemphill previously said the final series and stage show would be the "final nail in the final coffin".

They did adapt the series for a comic book , which was released in 2024.

In a statement, they said: "We had FOMO (Fear of moving on).

"Haud oan! Whit's been happenin? It's been far too lang…Craiglang."

The cast previously set a string of box-office records with their hugely popular live shows

Still Game first arrived on TV screens in 2002, although the characters of Jack and Victor previously featured in sketch show Chewin' the Fat.

Alongside old pals Winston Ingram, played by Paul Riley, tight-fisted Tam Mullen, played by Mark Cox, nosy Isa Drennan, played by Jane McCarry and shop owner Navid Harrid, played by Sanjeev Kohli, the comedy follows the lives of Jack and Victor as they navigate the fictional Glasgow suburb of Craiglang.

MN202611_1u87q6sznle.t:
Rooney scored 53 goals in 120 appearances for England

Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".

The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.

But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast , external , detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.

"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.

"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."

The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".

"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.

"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.

"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.

"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."

Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.

But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.

"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.

"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.

"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.

"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.

"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.

"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

The Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-upon-Avon Manuela Perteghella said plans to move the Shakespeare Institute to Birmingham are "shocking"

The MP for Stratford-upon-Avon has described plans to move the Shakespeare Institute to Birmingham as "ill-thought" and "shocking".

The postgraduate research institute is due to leave its historic home at Mason Croft and relocate to the University of Birmingham's Edgbaston campus in September.

The Liberal Democrat MP Manuela Perteghella said she would raise the issue in parliament and write to the university about her "deep disappointment" and concerns for the Institute's future.

"This is shocking and upsetting news for our town, which has deep connections with the institute. Its presence contributes not only to the cultural life of Stratford, but also to the local economy," she said.

The Shakespeare Institute announced on Friday that it had been told it would leave Stratford, with future plans unclear for its Mason Croft base, historic gardens and playing fields.

The body was launched under the university's auspices in 1951, based at Mason Croft, although it did temporarily move to Birmingham in the 1970s.

Perteghella said the institute had played a vital role in preserving Shakespeare's national and international legacy, and called it "callous" that staff and students had not been consulted.

The Shakespeare Institute was founded in 1951 at the Mason Croft building in Stratford-upon-Avon

The University of Birmingham said the move was "an academic decision" rather than a cost-cutting measure and insisted Shakespeare studies remained a priority.

It said the relocation was intended to secure the institute's "long-term future" and that current students, including postgraduate researchers, would be supported throughout the transition.

The university added it would consult the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC), the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, local representatives and the wider community in the coming weeks.

Perteghella is backing a petition launched by the Stratford Herald to keep the institute in the town , external . By Tuesday, it had attracted more than 12,000 signatures.

The petition calls on the university to retain the institute at Mason Croft, its Grade II listed home, and publish the rationale, financial data and equality impact assessments behind the decision.

Campaigners argue the move would damage Stratford's cultural and academic standing and threaten postgraduate Shakespeare studies in a town closely associated with William Shakespeare and the RSC.

The University of Birmingham said the move to relocate the centre was "an academic decision"

Actors Samuel West and Dame Janet Suzman have also backed the campaign.

In a joint statement, they said: "For 75 years, the Shakespeare Institute has stood at the heart of Stratford-upon-Avon, moments from Shakespeare's home, his church and the stages where his plays continue to be performed.

"To sever the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon and its home at Mason Croft is to destroy the very thing that makes it unique."

The Institute, which celebrated its 75th anniversary in July, has worked with academics, writers and performers for decades, including Dame Judi Dench.

The university said: "Mason Croft has been the Institute's home since 1951, and we are very mindful of its history.

"No decision has been taken on its future, and it remains the institute's home for this academic year."

MN202611_wm1domua5g.t:
Ally Fir says if a state scheme was running she'd "jump on it right away"

Lowering employers' National Insurance (NI) payments for those between 21 and 24, and cash incentives to take on some workers are among proposals put forward in Alan Milburn's report to get more 18-24 year-olds working.

Many companies have complained that recent increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to take on staff.

We talked to firms and business groups about the issues they face when hiring younger works and what they make of the proposals.

Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says he cannot justify the extra cost of training up new staff

Cutting NI costs is "right in the sweet spot of what firms need to hit the hire button", said the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC).

The Milburn report proposes NI thresholds could be raised over the next five years, from £5,000 to £10,000 for those aged 21 to 24, and suggests prioritising the retail and hospitality sectors.

Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says the high costs he faces currently make it difficult to employ young people with no work experience.

"My labour costs are already over 45%. We simply cannot justify the extra cost to put on an extra staff member to train someone up for three months," he says.

"In hospitality our margins have been squeezed and squeezed and squeezed"

As a result, he says it currently makes more sense to employ someone who already has experience.

Major report proposes welfare changes, apprenticeships and tax cuts to help 440,000 young people into work

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report

Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, says the recommendation to raise the threshold is "the right one" and "would be an immediate shot in the arm for job creation".

But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) argues the Milburn report does not go far enough in tackling costs facing businesses.

It says while the NI proposal is welcome, the change should be wider than just retail and hospitality, otherwise it "risks adding complexity and blocking off potential career paths".

Other proposals put forward by the Milburn review include cash incentives to employ younger workers.

Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet - not in education, employment or training - for six months should receive a £3,000 payment, and small businesses - with less than 50 employees - that do so should receive an extra £2,000

There would also be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled.

Ally Fir runs a bookshop in Westbourne, alongside her partner Matt, and thinks more state support is needed.

She says incentivised schemes for small business "would help us to employ more, especially young people. If a scheme like that was going we'd jump on it right away."

Fir says she gets job applications "every single day". She'd like to take more people on but "it is the cost of employing people that makes that impossible".

Tom Parsons has already had experience of using government schemes to employ young people at his design consultancy, Aetha, in Poole, Dorset.

The Kickstart Scheme in 2020 meant he could take on two young people in fully funded six-month job placements offering 25 hours a week.

Tom Parsons says the old Kickstart Scheme was a game-changer for those employed under it

"One of them stayed with us for five years and the other one I think about three years. And it completely changed the game for them", Tom told the BBC "so if there was a scheme like that, again, that would really help us".

He says he wants to employ young people but costs remain a huge barrier.

Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?

Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036

One of the government's flagship employment rights reforms risks weakening the hiring of young people, according to Milburn's report.

Ministers are abolishing what they call ''exploitative'' zero-hours contracts and replacing them with guaranteed hours contracts which would be based on the number of hours people normally work.

Much of the detail is yet to be finalised but the Employment Rights Act is due to be enacted next year.

Milburn is concerned that the changes could cause problems "at a time when the youth labour market is already weak'.'

The REC said companies were "particularly worried" over the guaranteed hours measure.

It added that addressing the Neets problem gave ministers "the perfect opportunity" to reconsider the issue.

Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee", Milburn has proposed.

This could help firms which are struggling to recruit. Thirty-five-year-old Dean Greene, a sales director at waste management facility Williams Environmental, says it's tricky finding staff.

"We didn't get many applicants for it at all," says Greene, referencing an ad for a marketing and sales role.

"There wasn't a huge uptake from that sort of 16-to-24 range," he adds.

He thinks the lack of applicants may be because the waste industry is perceived as "mucky and dirty", but he is confident many would be interested if they knew the job was available.

Pointing to himself as an example of progressing in the industry, he tells me how he started as an admin officer scanning paperwork at 18 before remaining with the company for 17 years.

MN202611_xnz6jes308.t:
The E1 area east of Jerusalem is a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank

The UK has sanctioned companies it said were involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.

The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.

Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.

It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.

The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".

The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.

It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.

The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of settlement goods and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.

Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.

"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.

"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.

"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."

UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response

Israel opens up bids for highly sensitive West Bank settlement project

In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

At the time, Miliband said the move marked the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering but acts".

The announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel .

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

England finished top of their Nations League group

England could host the Nations League finals this season after Football Association officials registered their interest.

The semi-final and finals of the competition, due to take place in June, are held in one country.

As well as England, it is understood that Spain and France have also contacted Uefa to register their interest in hosting the final four games, including the bronze medal match, which will run between 9-13 June.

The FA, it is understood, is still discussing potential venues with some doubt over whether Wembley would be available. The only publicly announced Wembley events in June are two concerts by singer Sam Fender, although these are for after the Nations League.

Thomas Tuchel's team will be seeded in Friday's draw for the quarter-finals following their euphoric 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, which secured top place in the group.

MN202611_wm7bsc0896.t:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge

Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.

A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.

The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.

For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff phased out air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November , when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.

But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.

In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.

One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.

The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk from the Royal United Services Institute said.

The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.

Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.

Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.

This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.

The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.

But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.

Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.

The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".

Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.

The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".

Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea – the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.

There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.

Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.

In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lays on the seabed.

Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

MN202611_151xngaqjx4.t:
Carney eyes 'other options' for embattled Canadian auto sector on China trip

The plight of Canada's car industry has become one of the clearest stress tests of Ottawa's effort to weather US tariffs and chart a path forward.

The past year and a half has been tough on the sector since US President Donald Trump imposed a 25% tariff on non-American-made vehicles, upending decades of free trade and automotive integration with Canada.

Now Prime Minister Mark Carney has signalled that he is looking to China, where he is on a visit for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit (Apec), as part of the solution.

But that avenue is not without controversy, and is once again drawing the ire of those close to Trump.

While in Cambodia earlier this week, Carney told reporters that Canada could turn to European and Asian carmakers to save its auto manufacturing sector if a trade deal with the US could not be reached.

"Look - great auto workers, important market, real assets in Canada," he said. "If they're not fully utilised in a North American context, that provides other opportunities.

"Canada's going to move forward either way."

He went on to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Tuesday for their second head-to-head in less than a year. The two talked afterwards of the importance of developing their relations, and Carney said they had agreed to further tariff cuts.

Neither side mentioned vehicles specifically, though analysts suggest the issue will have been prominent in their minds.

Carney and Xi met on Tuesday to discuss cooperation and trade ahead of this week's Apec summit

In January, Carney said that opening the door to China's electric vehicles , external (EV) could result in investment into Canadian-owned companies and the creation of manufacturing jobs in the sector.

American tariffs on imports of Canadian-made vehicles have led to thousands of job losses in Canada and anxiety over the future, as 90% of cars made in Canada are shipped to and sold in the US.

At the same time, China has been eyeing Canada as a potential entry-point to the North American EV market. Earlier this year, Canada announced that it would let in 49,000 EVs from China at a low tariff rate, with plans to raise that quota gradually to 70,000 by 2030.

The move was a significant break from the US, which has tariffed Chinese EVs heavily since the presidency of Joe Biden to protect domestic manufacturing.

Chinese EV manufacturers like BYD and Chery have already been lobbying the Canadian government for access.

Last week, Canada's Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu toured a Chery plant in China , external to discuss their potential entry to the Canadian market. He told reporters afterwards that Canadians could expect to see affordable Chinese electric vehicles for sale in Canada by early 2027.

Canada's international trade minister Maninder Sidhu toured a Chinese EV plant earlier this month

These moves come as the toll of US tariffs on Canada's auto sector has become harder to ignore.

Stellantis, an American car manufacturer that made models like the Dodge Challenger and the Chrysler 300 in Canada, recently announced it would sell its assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario - a move that Carney characterised as a "betrayal" of the plant's 2,200 workers.

The facility had been idle since 2023 for a planned retooling, but what was supposed to be a temporary shutdown became permanent after Trump's tariffs, leading the company to shift some manufacturing to Illinois in the US.

Stellantis said it would sell part of its Brampton plant to Roshel, a Canadian defence contractor and manufacturer of armoured vehicles.

The Canadian auto workers' union has expressed concern about the deal, calling it "underhanded" and warned that Canada would lose thousands of high-paying jobs as a result.

The deal has also led to speculation that a Chinese EV manufacturer could move into the facility, after Canadian media outlet CTV News reported , external , citing anonymous sources, that Stellantis was planning to lease back 25% of its plant to assemble "affordable" EVs.

Canada's deal with China signals it is serious about shift from US

How China made electric vehicles mainstream

There are prominent voices who oppose any such move, including within Canadian politics.

In a letter to Carney, Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned against opening the door for Chinese EV kits to be assembled in Canada at the Brampton plant.

China overwhelmingly builds its cars at home and ships them whole - or to be assembled in kits - overseas.

Lynette Ong, director of the China Governance Lab at the University of Toronto, said introducing Chinese auto manufacturing in Canada would be "controversial" due to fears that Canadian jobs could be lost and that the North American auto manufacturing industry could be eroded.

"We want to make sure they're hiring Canadian workers, that they are helping train Canadian workers and that they are transferring the technology over," Ong said.

She argued that Canada should also be wary of making itself vulnerable to potential security breaches and foreign interference from China, as well as risking the ire of the Trump administration.

That already appears to be happening. Peter Navarro, Trump's senior counsel for trade and manufacturing, warned Carney against cosying up to China in a post on X , external .

"Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme," he wrote on Monday. "You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive."

His comments were reposted by Pete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada.

Canadians' views of China have grown more positive since Trump's return to the White House. An Angus Reid poll released on Tuesday , external suggests many are open to Chinese investment in the EV sector, but with additional security or restrictions.

The Carney government has set terms for China's entry to Canada's auto market, including that any venture should be jointly-owned by a Canadian company, that it must follow Canadian labour standards and that the cars should be built using Canadian-made parts.

Ahead of his meeting with Xi on Tuesday, Carney also noted there are "clear guardrails" in how Canada deals with China, including barring work on sensitive matters like artificial intelligence and critical minerals.

Canada has also eyed other partnerships. It is notably pursuing associate member status with the EU, and had signed a free trade deal with the Philippines earlier this week.

Just how much Canada is willing to embrace Chinese manufacturing, however, still depends on the outcome of ongoing US-Canada trade talks.

Progress has been made in negotiations with the US, Carney recently said, but differences remain. It is unclear if Trump and Carney will speak on the sidelines of the Apec summit later this week.

MN202611_1094tk4xq0y.t:
BBC's Madeline Halpert explains why the US lost its measles elimination status and what it could mean.

After 26 years, the US has lost its status of having eliminated the highly contagious measles virus, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.

States have reported 10 measles-related deaths this year, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.

Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence of measles in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".

"These figures are a serious warning for our region," Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."

He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission.

The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.

Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards".

The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) did not respond to a request for comment from the BBC.

The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.

The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.

The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths.

But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems.

The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns.

The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity - which limits the spread of measles

The country has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, the most it has recorded in a year since 1991.

An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials.

US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database.

Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years.

Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics.

The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge.

Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections.

President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine.

Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates.

"It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."

The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

A York City FC player has appeared in court after allegedly punching a Rochdale AFC supporter during a pitch invasion.

Hiram Boateng, 30, of Leeds, pleaded not guilty at Manchester Magistrates' Court on Monday to using threatening, abusive or insulting behaviour with intent to cause fear of, or provoke, unlawful violence.

The charge relates to an incident involving fans who entered the pitch during the final-day match between the two sides at the Crown Oil Arena on 25 April.

York City FC said it was "aware of developments" following the incident and added Boateng, whose trial is due to begin on 23 June 2027, "maintains the full support of everyone at York City".

Rochdale supporters entered the pitch during the match after believing their side had secured the National League title. The alleged incident happened during a second pitch invasion later in the game.

A spokesperson for York City FC said: "We are aware of developments regarding the incident involving Hiram Boateng during the game against Rochdale in April.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing

The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.

Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.

Rather unusually, one of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.

The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.

They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.

Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.

The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.

"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate.

Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony.

Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land

Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries

Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters

Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution

Fix Our Climate: Ørsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind

The Earthshot prize, first held in 2020, was inspired by former US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

Tuesday's event also saw appearances on stage from Earthshot ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor.

As well as Take That, there were also musical performances from a number of Indian artists including Shreya Ghoshal, composer and pianist Merlin D'Souza and all-female hip hop collective Wild Wild Women.

The dazzling awards night was brought to a close by musician and composer Shashwat Sachdev.

After driving an electric rickshaw, William said he would've liked a longer promenade so he could "see what the top speed was"

Earlier on Tuesday, William and Catherine drove in an electric rickshaw to meet the 15 finalists.

As William stepped from the vehicle, which is manufactured by prize winner Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and has a top speed of 55mph, he said: "It was quite good fun, really good fun."

The couple arrived in India on Monday for the three-day visit, which is expected to also include a meeting with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.

Their first engagement saw them play a game of street - or "gully" cricket - in Mumbai alongside Tendulkar.

Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia, in his first public comments since his shock resignation.

"I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.

But he said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia.

As the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company.

The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely.

The company's board is investigating his conduct , which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive.

The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang.

Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead.

Nonetheless, Huang's statement appears to show some hope he will be able to move past the major corporate scandal.

Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics".

"If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added.

Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company.

Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return.

Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement.

On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course.

While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law."

Meet the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contenders

Voting for the BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year 2026 will close at 09:00 GMT on Wednesday, 18 November.

Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.

For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, 13 December as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.

Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-August 2026.

Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Temwa Chawinga

Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.

Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.

Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.

Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.

Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Ewa Pajor

Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.

Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.

The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.

Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.

On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland and is the team's leading goalscorer.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alexia Putellas

Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder

Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.

After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.

Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.

Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.

Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3–0.

Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alessia Russo

Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.

She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.

Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.

It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.

Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.

She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Khadija Shaw

After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.

The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.

Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.

They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.

She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.

Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

The US president was answering questions from reporters in the Philippines

President Donald Trump has said the US is taking "very seriously" the potential for any Iranian plot to attack Washington DC, after he was asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.

In the Philippines, where he attended the Asean Summit, Trump nodded when asked by a journalist about the report that Tehran was planning to detonate a so-called dirty bomb in the US capital and said: "We're looking into it."

CNN cited unnamed US intelligence officials suggesting Iran could target senior figures in Trump's administration with such an attack.

Iran called the claim "baseless." Concerns about dirty bombs grew after the 9/11 attacks in 2001, although no such attack has ever occurred.

Such a device would contain radioactive material - such as uranium - which would be scattered through the air when its conventional explosive detonated.

The BBC has not independently verified CNN's reporting.

During his comments to reporters in Manila, Trump was asked whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent.

"I hope it's not," he said, "but we take it very seriously because they [the Iranians] happen to be crazy."

In a statement before Trump's comments, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis wrote: "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei rebutted the CNN article and other US reports.

He posted on X: "Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations."

Mick Mulroy, a former CIA paramilitary officer and deputy assistant defence secretary, told the BBC: "A dirty bomb is not difficult to make or deploy."

"Although it is not a weapon of mass destruction, it can be a weapon of mass disruption," he added.

Imran Bayoumi, a geostrategy expert with the Atlantic Council in Washington DC and former policy adviser to the defence department, said that it remains "unclear how serious" would be the threat of a supposed Iranian dirty bomb.

"But Iran has planned and threatened to attack the US in the past," he said. "It is also unclear why this report is becoming public now."

It comes as intelligence officials and members of the Trump administration seek congressional renewal of a key national security law.

Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), which allows the US to ​spy on foreign nationals, expires next March.

Erasmus made the comments at a news conference in Dublin on Monday

South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been banned for six matches by World Rugby over comments he made about match officials in his side's Nations Championship defeat by France last week.

Speaking at a news conference conference in Dublin on Monday before the Springboks' match with Ireland, Erasmus questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "is that not match-fixing?".

The two-time Rugby World Cup-winning coach was referencing the implementation of new rules surrounding hip-drop and knee-drop tackles, and felt the laws were not being applied correctly.

It comes after Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast became the first player to be cited for a hip-drop tackle in Ireland's win over Fiji on Saturday , which was not penalised in-play by referee Angus Gardner and television match official [TMO] Mike Adamson.

World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments "suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match".

In response, South Africa Rugby said it has requested a full misconduct hearing and an opportunity for Erasmus to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".

It is the third time Erasmus has been sanctioned by World Rugby over his comments about match officials.

When he was South Africa's director of rugby, he was suspended for two months by World Rugby after he posted an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' opening Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions in 2021.

World Rugby found the video contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials".

In 2022, he received a two-match ban for a series of tweets criticising officials in a defeat by France.

Erasmus' latest ban has been imposed under World Rugby's match official abuse sanction process, which was introduced by the governing body in July.

If the suspension is upheld, Erasmus will miss Saturday's game with Ireland in Dublin (16:40 GMT), next week's finals weekend fixture at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium and the start of his side's Rugby Championship campaign next summer.
