Erasmus said that 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles had been missed in South Africa's 21-19 defeat in France by match officials. Andrea Piardi was the referee for the Stade de France fixture, while Matteo Liperini was the TMO.

Erasmus added that if TMOs were not intervening for reviews to limit the number of interruptions during a match then it was "manipulation", before he added that his comments were "not an accusation".

"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.

"If the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured.

"So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

In a statement on Tuesday, World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments had met "the threshold for serious misconduct".

World Rugby confirmed the ban will stop Erasmus having any match day involvement for six matches, which includes coaching, direct or indirect contact with the team management or players on match days, entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure or technical area.

"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," its statement said.

"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity.

"Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension."

Erasmus' Springboks side lost 21-19 to France in Stade de France on Friday night

World Rugby added that "respect is fundamental to rugby, and match officials are central to the sport".

"Protecting their wellbeing and integrity, and their right to perform without abuse or intimidation, is a responsibility World Rugby and unions take seriously," their statement added.

"Coaches, players, unions and everyone in the game must uphold these standards.

"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches. Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."

In the same news conference, which lasted more than half an hour at the Springboks' team hotel, Erasmus also questioned what he felt were double standards in terms of sanctions.

The outcome of the citing has yet to be released, but he predicted that Prendergast will be available to play against South Africa due to a "technicality", and also questioned the decision not to ban Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong for an alleged groin grab while playing for Leinster ahead of the November Tests.

Last year, South Africa prop Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-match ban for a similar offence and missed November's matches for the Springboks.

This is the third time in five years Erasmus has been banned for comments about referees, all of them coming after a Springboks loss.

In 2018, he picked South African rugby up off the floor and has won two World Cups to establish himself as one of the greatest coaches of all time.

To his rugby public - the people who really matter in Erasmus' eyes - he will forever be a hero in his homeland.

But outside South Africa his propensity to harangue officials after a rare defeat will tarnish his reputation in the eyes of many.

The film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.

IndieWire , external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".

The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.

The New York Times , external also used the word "slog", explaining: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't.

"In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."

However, the Hollywood Reporter , external was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".

Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."

And Time Out's four-star review , external said the film is "as strong as any" of the other movies, and "certainly a major step up from 2023's drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes".

Former Arsenal and England midfielder Peter Storey has died at the age of 81.

Storey made 501 appearances in all competitions for the Gunners between 1965 and 1977, scoring 17 goals.

He was part of the Double-winning Arsenal team which secured the First Division title and FA Cup in 1970-71 under manager Bertie Mee.

"Everyone at Arsenal is deeply saddened by the passing of double winner Peter Storey," Arsenal said in a statement.

"All our thoughts are with his family and loved ones at this incredibly sad time.

"We will pay our respects to Peter at our forthcoming home match against Borussia Dortmund."

Surrey-born Storey joined Arsenal as an apprentice in 1961 and made his first-team debut against Leicester City in 1965, initially starting his career at right-back before being moved into midfield.

He is currently eighth on Arsenal 's list of all-time appearance holders and was capped 19 times by England, although he did not feature in a major tournament for the Three Lions.

Storey collected runners-up medals with Arsenal in the League Cup in 1967-68 and 1968-69 and in the FA Cup in 1971-72.

He joined Second Division Fulham on a free transfer in March 1977 and made 19 appearances for the Cottagers before his contract was terminated later that year and he retired.

However, Storey had something of a troubled life after his retirement from professional football.

He was convicted of running a brothel - for which he received a suspended prison sentence in 1979 - and was later jailed for three years for his involvement in a counterfeiting operation, then served another prison sentence in 1990 for attempting to smuggle pornographic videos into Britain.

Masha was in her kitchen when she heard the explosions blast through the city

The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.

Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.

Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.

At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.

The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.

Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.

Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.

Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.

"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.

But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.

"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."

The Northern Bridge crossing is closed to traffic while emergency response teams work to clear the debris

From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.

A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.

Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.

The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.

On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.

"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."

The main bridges over the River Dnipro - that cuts through Kyiv - were the target of Russian strikes

That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.

Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.

Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.

To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.

But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.

The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.

"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

At the height of his career, Baker made six first-team appearances for Brighton under former manager Roberto de Zerbi, including in the Premier League.

The England Under-20 international also spent time in the academy systems at West Ham and Porto before making 14 senior appearances on loan as Port Vale finished second in League Two in 2024.

Nearly eight in every 10 people living in the East African Community (EAC) are below the age of 35, with the region’s population reaching an estimated 361.1 million in 2026, according to new figures released by the EAC Secretariat.

The figures show that 77.1% of the regional population is below 35, highlighting the growing importance of education, employment, healthcare, housing and other services as East Africa’s population expands.

Women account for 50.1% of this younger population, according to the report, which also shows that the EAC added 47.5 million people between 2021 and 2026, representing a 15.1% increase.

The regional population grew by approximately 9.6 million people in the past year alone, equivalent to an annual increase of 2.7%.

The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is the most populous EAC Partner State, with 123.2 million people, representing 34.1% of the regional population.

Tanzania follows with 70 million people, ahead of Kenya’s 54.2 million and Uganda’s 49.6 million. Together, the four countries account for 82.3% of the Community’s population.

Somalia has an estimated population of 19.3 million, followed by South Sudan with 16.4 million, Rwanda with 14.4 million and Burundi with 13.9 million.

Population growth has been faster in some countries than others. Between 2021 and 2026, South Sudan recorded the highest increase at 19.7%, followed by Tanzania at 17.8%, DRC at 17.1% and Uganda at 15.6%. Kenya recorded the slowest growth, at 9.1%.

The report also highlights the scale of the region’s young population. Children below 15 account for 43.2% of the EAC population, with 59.7 million children aged between zero and four years. This is about a third more than the 44.8 million aged between 10 and 14, pointing to continued demand for schools, teachers and learning materials as younger children grow.

Meanwhile, the EAC’s youth population, defined as people aged 15 to 35 in line with the African Youth Charter, increased from 106.6 million in 2021 to 126.9 million in 2026. Young people now represent 35.1% of the regional population, with females accounting for 50.6%.

The working-age population, comprising people aged 15 to 64, reached 193.7 million, or 53.7% of the total population, up from 166.1 million in 2021.

The EAC says this growing working-age population presents an opportunity for economic development, provided countries invest in skills and create productive employment. The potential economic benefit is known as a demographic dividend.

However, the region continues to face the challenge of supporting a large dependent population. The age dependency ratio declined from 88.8% in 2021 to 86.4% in 2026, meaning there are approximately 86 people below 15 or aged 65 and above for every 100 people of working age.

The EAC Vision 2050 targets a reduction in unemployment from 14% in 2014 to 10% by 2030 and 5% by 2050.

The report also notes that population density increased from 61 people per square kilometre in 2021 to 71 in 2026, across the Community’s approximately 5.1 million square kilometres of land.

Beyond the younger population, women and girls account for 183.1 million people, or 50.7% of the EAC population. Meanwhile, people aged 60 and above number approximately 17.2 million, representing 4.7% of the regional population.

The Secretariat says reliable population statistics are essential for planning public services and distributing resources. It estimates that 40% of the Community’s population was not enumerated during the 2020 Census Round covering 2015–2024.

In June 2024, the EAC Secretariat launched efforts to harmonise population and demographic statistics and subsequently developed regional guidelines for population and housing censuses.

The Community is now advocating a common census theme and topics for the 2030 Census Round, while encouraging all Partner States to conduct a census.

JJ Gabriel scored a hat-trick on his last appearance for Manchester United in September before walking out on the club

JJ Gabriel has confirmed his exit from Manchester United with a farewell video message in which he says the club will "will always be part of my story".

The 16-year-old forward, who has a verbal agreement to join Spanish giants Real Madrid, walked out on United in September.

He has subsequently been training on his own in Spain after relocating with his family.

The 50-second video montage, posted on social media, begins with Gabriel penning a letter to United, and includes some of his notable achievements, including coming on for his first-team debut during a pre-season friendly with Atletico Madrid in Stockholm in August, when he was just 15.

Gabriel then thanks United's coaches and staff, plus his team-mates as he "begins my next chapter".

He has not returned to United since scoring a hat-trick in a Uefa Youth League game with Sabah in September.

Although United still hold the teenager's registration until the end of the season, it does not prevent him moving to a club in the European Union as he now has an EU passport through his mother, who is of Cypriot heritage.

Speaking to Spanish newspaper Marca earlier this month, he said his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

However, Gabriel has now broken his silence on his controversial decision to leave United, having won last season's Premier League Under-18 player of the year award, United's U18 player of the year award and been top scorer in a side that reached the FA Youth Cup final and Premier League U18 cup final.

"I arrived in 2020 as a 10-year-old boy with big dreams. Here, I grew as a player and a person, from scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy [Under-18] award . You gave me moments I will always treasure.

"To every coach, every member of staff, to my team-mates and everyone who supported me; thank you for believing in me and helping me grow. As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be part of my story.

The US serviceman is understood to have been based at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire

A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.

The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who has served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.

Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, which serves as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC).

Counter Terror Policing said he has since been taken into custody by the US military over suspected national security and espionage allegations.

British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.

FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners.

"Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said.

"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."

US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take.

"Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

Pedro Sánchez (left), Alberto Núñez Feijóo (centre) and Santiago Abascal (right)

Spanish voters face a snap election on 29 November, with the conservatives and the far right favourites to win after eight years of Socialist-led rule under Pedro Sánchez.

The left had hoped to focus on Spain's housing crisis, but the government has been buffeted by corruption scandals, a migrant crisis, and most recently rail disasters that left 115 people dead. Here are the key figures to look out for in the race to run Spain's next government.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) tops most of the polls and as leader of the conservative opposition since 2022 he is favourite to become Spain's next prime minister.

His pitch to voters is his experience and reputation as a capable administrator, with 13 years as president of the north-west Galicia region from 2009.

"It's called management: and it's what I know how to do, it's what I want to do, and it's the change Spain needs," he has told voters.

Feijóo has held public office continuously since 1991, and although he guided the PP to win the biggest number of seats in parliament in 2023, they fell short of an outright parliamentary majority. Sánchez's Socialist PSOE stayed in power through deals with left-wing parties and the backing of Catalan and Basque nationalist parties and pro-independence groups.

Feijóo says the best outcome for Spain would be a PP majority governing alone, with support in parliament from far-right party Vox. His party has worked in coalition with Vox in four Spanish regions, and he has not ruled out a national coalition under strict conditions and red lines.

Unlike Sánchez, the PP leader is not well known internationally and his lack of English may hold him back on the world stage. Feijóo admits to making little effort to learn English but believes the "enormous problems" faced by Spaniards are of greater importance: "I don't know English, but I know how to govern."

Sánchez has led the Socialists for the past 12 years, and Spain since 2018.

He has built a reputation as a political survivor but this election - his sixth in 11 years - could be his toughest yet.

Sánchez called the snap election eight months early , seeking to focus on resolving Spain's housing crisis, and vowing "an epic comeback of a progressive Spain" at the ballot box.

But he and his party have been embroiled in a series of corruption scandals, a migrant crisis in Spain's Ceuta exclave on the Moroccan border and two deadly rail disasters nine months apart. The most recent tragedy claimed 69 lives at Urda on 28 October and overshadowed the start of the campaign.

The Socialist leader has been written off in politics before, only to stage comebacks, notably in 2017 and 2023.

He can point to a projected 2.6% annual growth in the Spanish economy in 2026, fuelled by tourism, but the graft cases against his inner circle and family are not going away.

José Luis Ábalos, who was transport minister in Sánchez's government, is now serving a 24-year prison sentence for accepting kickbacks, meanwhile leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.

Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, faces trial over allegations of influence peddling and embezzlement while his brother, David Sánchez, has been banned from public office for nine years for misconduct. Both deny doing anything wrong.

In a defiant message, Begoña Gómez made her first party speech at the Socialist campaign launch, calling for the backing of Spanish women, "because when women step forward, all of Spain follows".

Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike

Sánchez's fate could be sealed by the rise of Abascal's anti-immigration, populist Vox - with opinion polls putting them in a comfortable third place and taking votes from the Socialists.

Abascal, 50, denies his party is far-right and has succeeded in bringing Vox into the mainstream, attracting record ratings on one of Spanish state TV's primetime entertainment shows during the campaign.

Repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain are big themes for Abascal, who has accused Pedro Sánchez of promoting an "act of invasion" with his policies.

He has promised to use the Spanish navy to defend the national borders and "send a message to the world that there is no room here for all of Africa and all of the Americas".

The Vox leader joined the PP aged 18, becoming a local councillor first and then an MP in the Basque regional parliament.

His political trajectory was closely shaped by his family's experience of threats and intimidation by Basque militant group Eta. Both his father and grandfather, who held public office, were targeted because of their political roles.

He left the conservatives in 2013, founding Vox the following year and becoming a Spanish MP in 2019, when Vox became the first hard-right party in decades to establish a significant presence in Congress.

Vox has adopted the Trump-inspired slogan "Make Spain Great Again" and advocates a strongly centralised vision of the country strongly opposed to the independence movement in Catalonia.

Critics have described the party's ideology as reminiscent of aspects of the era of dictator Francisco Franco era, which Vox rejects.

Former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Frente Amplio (Broad Front) - which has lost many of its supporters in recent weeks to the Socialists and is currently polling in fourth place.

Previously called Sumar, the coalition was in government with the Socialists under leader Yolanda Díaz, but she decided she would not run again. Colau came into politics as a housing activist and fair rents and housing is one of her coalition's big policies.

Irene Montero of Podemos and the pro-Catalan independence ERC party of Gabriel Rufián have combined forces in a bid to gain more seats

Other parties on the left are contesting the election separately, including the pro-Catalan independence Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya (ERC) under Gabriel Rufián who has reached a campaign deal with Podemos under Irene Montero .

Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies

Catalan centre-right pro-independence party Junts per Catalunya played a pivotal role in supporting Pedro Sánchez's government, even though it had just seven seats in the 350-seat Congress, and it may be central to post-election negotiations too. It was Junts' decision to reject the government's housing proposals last month that pushed the Socialist leader into snap elections.

Its lead candidate is Míriam Nogueras, who has made clear that Catalan demands come first for her party. Junts president Carles Puigdemont, 63, is planning to return to Spain after the election. He has lived in self-imposed exile since 2017 after leading Catalonia's failed bid for independence.

Analysts see Madrid's regional leader Isabel Díaz Ayuso as a possible candidate for prime minister in the future

Isabel Díaz Ayuso , 48, has been president of the Madrid region since 2019 and has become one of the most influential figures within the People's Party. She leads one of the PP's strongest electoral bastions, with conservatives having ruled the region for the past 31 years.

Ayuso has built a distinct political profile that often sets her apart from the party establishment. Her direct communication style and informal use of language have helped her connect with voters and attract significant media attention.

Her tenure has not been without controversy. Her partner has been the subject of a judicial investigation relating to alleged tax offences and document forgery, allegations he denies.

Opposition parties have also questioned the Madrid regional government's purchase of a luxury penthouse for official use. Critics have challenged the rationale behind the acquisition, while regional authorities have maintained that it was intended as a government workspace.

Socialist Carlos Cuerpo , 46, was chosen by Pedro Sánchez to take charge as interim transport minister after the Urda rail disaster and has become key to his election team. Cuerpo climbed the ranks through the economy ministry and became minister of economy, trade and business in 2023.

He has been ranked as best-regarded politician among the Spanish public, according to the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), and, when asked about his political ambitions has called himself "a team player, and I am committed to the team".

In the same light, Sánchez has said: "I believe politics is a team sport; on the opposing team we have Feijóo and Abascal, and on my team we have Carlos Cuerpo."

Catalonia's Socialist president Salvador Illa is also one to watch. He served as Spain's health minister during the Covid pandemic and some have viewed him as a potential successor as Socialist leader, even though he has backed Sánchez to remain as leader.

A close ally to Sánchez, Salvador Illa (L) is often named as possible successor

Carlos Hernández Quero , 30, has been a Vox MP since 2023, and speaks for the party on housing and urban affairs, taking charge of one of the most important election issues.

He is not regarded as the party's second-in-command, a position more commonly associated with figures such as Montserrat Lluís or Ignacio Garriga , but he is media-savvy and known for his clear, combative defence of Vox's economic policies and proposals.

Further to the right is Alvise Pérez , 36, a Member of the European Parliament who leads Se Acabó la Fiesta (The party is over). His party won three seats in European elections in 2024 and attracts voters disappointed with Vox. His party adopts a hard line on immigration, corruption and the EU.

Rangers say Ralph Brand will "forever be remembered as a great of the club"

Rangers have paid tribute to Ralph Brand, one of the most prolific goalscorers in the club's history, who has died aged 89.

A Hall of Fame forward at Ibrox, the former Scotland striker, who scored eight times in eight caps, netted 222 goals in 347 appearances for the Govan side.

Brand joined Rangers as a 17-year-old in 1952 before going on to play for the first team for 13 years, until 1965.

He was part of four league-winning sides and won three Scottish Cups and four Scottish League Cups during his time at Ibrox.

After spells in England with Manchester City and Sunderland, Brand returned to Scotland to finish his playing career with Raith Rovers and Hamilton Academical.

"Ralph Brand's contribution to Rangers was vast and, through his Hall of Fame recognition, he will forever be remembered as a great of the club," the Ibrox club said in a statement.

The legal action against Natural Resources Wales landed in the High Court

River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.

River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.

It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital" .

NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".

The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.

The three farms are Neuadd Isaf, Rhosddu and Llanshay.

Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.

Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.

The three poultry units in Powys are located within river catchments including the River Wye

Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.

Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.

Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.

Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.

River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.

Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, argues there is a "regulatory gap" in the management of off-site manure

Campaigners set up a chicken-themed protest outside the High Court hearing in Llandrindod Wells on Tuesday.

"River Action will argue that Natural Resources Wales has the power to address and assess the impact of that manure on the environment and, as the specialist regulator, should be lawfully deciding how to use that power when operating the permitting regime," said Julia Eriksen, of solicitors Leigh Day, representing River Action.

The organisation insisted NRW could put controls on the farm's permit to reduce or remove the risk of manure causing pollution.

Campaigners believe the birds' manure will spread on fields and into rivers, causing harm

Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, said NRW "decided that it didn't have the power to look at what would happen when a lot of the manure would go offsite" when the plans were approved last year.

"That matters because more chickens means more muck, and that needs to go somewhere and someone has to deal with it," she said.

"So this case is all about making NRW realise that it does have the power to deal with it."

An NRW spokesperson said: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on matters that are before the court. We will continue to participate fully in the legal process and await the court's determination."

Firefighter Steve Williams, pictured here with his widow Jilska, died of a rare lung cancer 14 years after falling into a toxic lagoon

It was a sight which struck terror into the firefighters called to tackle it - a blazing chemical waste lagoon on fire, with barrels exploding into the air.

Steve Williams, then in his 20s, was one of 60 firefighters sent to tackle the burning Llwyneinion lagoon in August 1980, which was sending thick black smoke over a nearby village.

Steve slipped in and, although he was pulled out, his widow thinks what he swallowed may have cost him his life from a rare form of lung cancer aged 39. She said "someone should be held accountable".

Wrexham council, which owns the site, said while it did not meet the legal definition of "contaminated land", it regularly inspected and monitored the area.

It took 60 firefighters about 18 hours to bring the 1980 fire at Llwyneinion lagoon under control

A leading expert in fire chemistry and toxicity said it was difficult to establish a link between firefighters' exposure to chemicals and health issues later in life.

Steve's widow Jilska Williams believes the father-of-two's terminal cancer could have stemmed from the chemicals at the fire at the former toxic waste dump near Wrexham in north Wales.

"It's a definite probability," said the 71-year-old. "They're firemen and they're always running into fires, so you don't know what the long-term effects are going to be - but actually falling into the lake and drinking that fluid, which is full of chemicals. He had a double-whammy, didn't he?"

Steve's family are part of a group which came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.

This is the last family photo of Jilska and Steve Williams, with their children David and Kelly, taken in June 1994, shortly before he was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer

They want surviving firefighters to be tested for deadly carcinogens they fear they were exposed to in the fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon.

Eleven firefighters or their families have told a BBC investigation about concerns the fire could have had an impact on their health.

They said there was an increased number of miscarriages suffered by partners of those who attended the fire in the year after - and also highlighted concerns about rates of cancers since.

Steve followed his dad into the fire service in 1978 and his first posting was in Wrexham, where he was among the first responders to the lagoon fire.

What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales.

Jilska said he was checked at hospital after falling in, then given a tetanus injection before being sent home.

"What is a tetanus injection going to do for him?" said the retired nurse. "It was a disaster waiting to happen. A time bomb waiting to go off, as far as I'm concerned."

The couple moved to Melbourne in Australia, then in 1994 Steve was diagnosed with stage four cancer – small cell carcinoma - and given weeks to live.

He died three days after the couple's 17th wedding anniversary. Their children were aged six and 10.

The Llwyneinion site was a dumping ground for chemicals suspected to have included cancer-causing polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) from chemical giant Monsanto.

Sheen's Buried programme team found elevated levels of PCBs in soil samples taken in an area open to the public beyond the fenced-off lagoon, as well as at 13 other suspected dumpsites for the firm's toxic waste across the country.

Footage from a BBC news report in August 1980 shows the extent of the toxic waste dump fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon

PCBs were once widely used in things like lipsticks and white goods - and were liked for being non-flammable and hard to break down.

But today they are seen as the first "forever chemicals" which are building up in the environment, threatening wildlife and human health.

The Llwyneinion lagoon was purchased by the then Clwyd County Council for just £1 in May 1980.

Andy Moore spent the day bringing in foam to help firefighters smother the fire at the former dump - and saw Steve fall in.

Andy, who was also stationed at Wrexham, said firefighters were not equipped to face the chemicals in the lagoon.

Steve Williams, on the left, and Andy Moore, on the right, were stationed at Wrexham fire station

"There was no request for chemical PPE, we were basically fighting that fire in our normal tunics, drips and helmets," said Andy, now 70.

"I was walking around that fire ground in a shirt and tie - I've always been concerned about what it could have done to me.

"I was diagnosed a year ago with skin cancer.

"Whether I can relate that back to this specific incident I don't know but there's too many coincidences - I talk to my colleagues and we've had a lot of our guys who have died young specifically of cancers."

The lagoon at Llwyneinion is one of 12 locations around Wales that were highlighted as historic toxic waste dumping grounds of concern in Michael Sheen's BBC documentary Buried

Jim MacGrane was also a firefighter at Wrexham at that time and his wife suffered a miscarriage in the period after the fire.

"There were six wives that we can recall had miscarriages within 12 to 15 months of that incident," said Jim, now 71.

"It was highlighted by one of the guys on the station who said, 'that's not coincidence. There's something not right there'."

Mark Jones and his father Ken both attended the fire and Ken later died of lymph and brain cancer in 2011.

Mark Jones and his father Ken were firefighters in Wrexham and attended the toxic waste dump fire at Llwyneinion Lake

"Out of the 60 people that attended that fire a significant number had cancers or passed away with cancer," said Mark, now 68.

"I'd be keen to participate in some blood testing to see if there was any link because it's only recently we found out about the PCBs in the vicinity.

"We were fairly well looked after health-wise when we were in the service, we used to have an annual health check. Unfortunately once you've finished the service that doesn't continue."

Professor Anna Stec, one of the UK's leading experts on fire chemistry and toxicity, warned it would be challenging to prove a firefighter's exposure to particular chemicals during their career had led to health issues later in life.

A group of former Wrexham firefighters who attended the Llwyneinion lagoon fire came forward to raise their concerns about the blaze

"It's very difficult to link specific chemicals to health disorders and it requires a multi-disciplinary approach where we're looking at residents' exposure, their lifestyle, and so on," said the University of Leicester professor.

"With firefighters it's even harder," she added, as they can be exposed to "a cocktail of toxic substances" throughout their careers.

But Stec said there should be more research into what happened at Llwyneinion.

"What we're learning from our Firefighters' Cancer and Disease Registry is that we see a pattern where there is a major fire incident - and a group of firefighters developing similar cancers. So it's definitely worth looking at."

The Llwyneinion lagoon is still there, but fenced off, which has worried some of the firefighters.

"The actual lagoon is still there from what I can make out in the same state it was 46 years ago," said Stuart Jones. "The potential of that happening again is very clear."

Steve Williams with his mum Phyllis, who visited from Rhyl while he was dying in Australia, and his two children Kelly and David

The BBC has been told the group of Llwyneinion firefighters are set to meet with representatives from the Fire Brigades' Union (FBU) later this week.

"We're taking this really seriously," said Gareth Tovey of the FBU.

He said the union was consulting with scientists to "discuss what options we may have available to support" the retired firefighters in their search for answers.

Tovey said he would write to Wales' fire and rescue services to ask about protections in place today for those called to attend an incident at sites linked to historical dumping of toxic waste.

Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond when asked to comment.

Wrexham Council said while the site did not meet the legal definition of "contaminated land" under current legislation, there were regular inspections of the surrounding area and ongoing monitoring of streams and groundwater.

"The council is sorry to hear of the illnesses experienced by members of the fire service and their families," said a council spokesperson.

The lagoon at Llwyneinion is still there today but is surrounded by a fence

The council said it took "its responsibilities for protecting public health and the environment extremely seriously" and had carried out "extensive investigations over many years" into the Llwyneinion lagoon.

Wrexham council added that concerns about the health of firefighters who attended the fire were raised with their contaminated land officer twice.

The first was in February 2004 by the fire officer in charge at Wrexham fire station and on another occasion by a fire officer, who was told to speak to the health authority.

On the risk of another fire on the site, Wrexham council said that in 2006 advice was sought from the fire service about this, but they were told a number of "specific circumstances" would need to occur for this to happen.

An emergency response plan has been drawn up, and it was revisited in 2017.

North Wales Fire and Rescue Service said it was not in a position to comment on the fire in 1980.

It added: "We recognise the importance of understanding the potential long-term health impacts associated with firefighting. Approaches to occupational health, wellbeing and health monitoring continue to be developed nationally as evidence, research and understanding across the sector evolve."

The Welsh government announced in its draft budget on Tuesday that it would commit £2m to "kick-start a new approach to managing contaminated land".

"We are developing a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land," the government said in a statement.

"We also continue to press the UK government for funding to address the legacy of Wales's industrial past, including the remediation of contaminated land."

Nvidia's now former CEO Jensen Huang had become a face of the AI boom.

Nvidia's interim chief executive Collette Kress said the company's rapid growth remains on track despite the dramatic exit of founder Jensen Huang.

In her first public comments since Huang plunged the multi-trillion dollar chip manufacturer into chaos, Kress said Nvidia's "roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater".

The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, topping $100bn for the first time, with shares in the company climbing in after-hours trading.

Earlier on Tuesday Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following two alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a possible spy for China.
